blocks.text: The record

Eastern and southern Australia share one wholesale electricity market. Every generator, battery and large flexible load tells the market operator, AEMO, how much power it will supply at each step of a ladder of prices. The prices on the ladder are fixed the day before. The volume offered at each step can still be moved until shortly before the power is needed. Each such move is a rebid. The operator's software then chooses the cheapest workable set of offers and sets a price for each region, interval by interval.

The market rules say each rebid must come with a brief, verifiable and specific reason [ner-3822]. The published table holds the reason as a short line of text, a one-letter category (plant, a change in the operator's forecast or instructions, commercial, or error) and the times of the event the trader relied on [mms-model]. All of it is released the next day.

An illustration, not a real file: at 9:35 in the morning the operator's forecast of Queensland demand rises from 2,400 to 2,600 megawatts. A trader at a gas plant moves 150 megawatts from the $300 step down to the $60 step so the plant will be called on, and files the reason "0935 A 30-MIN PD FORECAST DEMAND INCREASE 2400 2600". Minutes later the public tables show how much the plant was told to generate and what the region's price was. So one record is the state of the market beforehand, the move, a one-line reason, and what the market then paid.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for practice tasks with a check that is hard to game. Here the check is a market price. The record could only be useful as a practice setting, where a system places bids against a replay of a past day and is scored on the money they would have earned, or as a private test. As raw data it has little value, because anyone may download it.
No purchase of an energy-market practice setting by a lab or a vendor was found.
Who holds it and who may share it
AEMO publishes the bids. Its copyright notice gives a general permission for anyone to use AEMO material "for any purpose", provided it is attributed accurately [aemo-copyright].

Two loose ends remain. The general terms of use on the same website speak of personal use, or use as authorised, and point to the permission notice [aemo-legal]; the two pages sit awkwardly together. And the reason text is written by the trader, not by AEMO or on its behalf. Whether the permission reaches that text was not established.
Traders' own internal logs are fuller than the published line and are not public.
The energy regulator reports that rebids grew from 5.4 million a year in 2020 [aer-2026] to 73 million in 2025 [aer-2026].
Who is already there

A university group has released free tools that download the bid tables, chart bids by plant, and replay the market. The replay tool's documentation says it can recreate past dispatch closely from the public bids [nempy]. The hard part of a practice setting, the engine, is therefore already free.

Researchers have studied rebids for years: a consultant's report for the market's rule-maker [roam], a journal study in 2016 [energy-econ-2016] and public code covering a decade of rebidding [rebid-analysis]. A 2024 paper tuned a language model on participants' bids to forecast prices; only its abstract was read [llm-bids-2024].

Free tests of AI systems on electricity markets exist for Texas [ercot-bench], for battery trading with language-model agents [alphasearch], for several American markets [energyagentbench] and for Europe [bessbidder]. Commercial auto-bidding software already does the live job for batteries.
Nobody was found packaging the reason text itself.
What would have to be stripped
Nothing, by design: the record describes plants and companies. Whether some reason lines carry a trader's initials was not checked.
What stands in the way

items: The data is free to everyone and the replay engine is open source, so nothing here can be held exclusively.
The reasons are thin. The regulator's own template is a time, a category letter and a few words [aer-guideline], and a practitioner's guide says they are often vague [mdavis].

Most reasons are now written by software. The regulator says automated bidding accounts for the vast majority of rebids by renewable and battery plants [aer-bulletin-2026]. It opened a review of its rebidding guideline in March 2026 that canvasses the use of artificial intelligence in bidding [aer-consult-2026].

Scoring is contestable for any plant large enough to move the price, because the replay must then guess how rivals would have responded. The replay tool is documented only for repeating history, not for changing one participant's bids.
Demand for energy trading in particular is voiced by a middleman, not a buyer.

blocks.text: The record

A toll road, wind farm or hospital built with borrowed money is sized from one large spreadsheet, the financial model, built by the project's backers or their adviser. Before the banks sign, an independent firm called a model auditor checks it. The auditor reads the formulas or rebuilds the results by another method, compares the model with the loan and project contracts and with tax and accounting rules, and sends back a numbered list of issues. The modeller fixes them and sends a new version. This repeats until the list is closed and the auditor signs a letter the lenders can rely on.
One case is therefore a chain: first version, first issue list, second version, second list, and so on to a final model and an opinion.

A real example, from a report a British health regulator published in its committee papers. In 2013 the firm Mazars reviewed two [hcpc-2013] revenue-forecast models for the regulator. It built its own shadow model and ran software tests. After the first review there were three [hcpc-2013] further rounds. In all the firm raised 68 [hcpc-2013] comments, each placed in one of three [hcpc-2013] grades, from a possible material error down to information only, and each marked open or closed. None fell in the most serious grade. The opinion covered only the fourth [hcpc-2013] version. An audit for a project loan follows the same steps at larger scale.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for work in spreadsheets and for fixes to real failures. Finding an unnamed error in a spreadsheet is something current systems do badly. A public test released in 2026 has a debugging section where the system must find and repair errors nobody has pointed out. The best system tested got 12.00% [ssb2] of those tasks right, against 34.89% [ssb2] across the whole test.
An audit file would supply the missing answer key: errors a professional confirmed, and the corrected version.
One of that test's authors is a data vendor [ssb2], so vendors already make expert-built spreadsheet tasks. Nobody was found selling real audit files.
Who holds it and who may share it

A few firms do most of the work. Forvis Mazars says it has given opinions on more than 2,000 [mazars-audit] project models and employs over 100 [mazars-audit] model auditors. Its Sydney team was formerly an independent firm, bought in 2016 [mazars-corality]. Operis says it audits over a hundred [operis] models a year and backs each opinion with a liability cap of up to £20 million [operis]. BDO in Britain says it has supported over 2,500 [bdo] projects.
The model belongs to the project's backers or the borrower. The issue list and working papers are the auditor's own product. The opinion is addressed to named lenders.

The published 2013 report states that it is confidential, is not to go beyond the addressees of the engagement letter, and may not be disclosed to others without the firm's written consent [hcpc-2013]. That points to at least two consents for a real file, the auditor's and the owner's, with the lenders' confidentiality terms on top. No engagement letter for a project-loan audit was opened, so the exact terms were not established.
Who is already there

The 2026 spreadsheet test has 321 [ssb2] tasks and a debugging section built, its authors say, from real business data with errors marked by experts. Its models are company accounts with errors planted in them, not project-loan models with real findings.
A second test, published the same year, draws 172 [finch] working sequences from old corporate files; the best system passed 38.4% [finch].
One data vendor publishes a finance question set and says its tasks are written by people from large investment banks [afterquery].
The auditors themselves sell review software and training. None was found selling data.
What no public set holds is a real project-loan model with its real numbered findings and the corrected version. The wider idea, spreadsheet debugging with expert-confirmed errors, is taken.
What would have to be stripped

There is no personal information. The sensitive content is commercial: tariffs, margins and returns that can identify a project even with the names removed. A model rebuilt closely enough from a real deal to be recognised carries the same problem as the original.
What stands in the way

items: The real file sits behind the owner's rights, the auditor's liability and the lenders' confidentiality terms.
A version rebuilt by experts is lawful but is the same kind of goods vendors already sell, and labs mark down contrived tasks.
The pool of people who have done this work is small, and most are employed by the firms that hold the files.
A published low score invites every vendor to aim at it, so the gap may not last.

blocks.text: The record
Accounting work is checked in layers: a junior prepares the file, a senior marks what is wrong, the junior answers, and the file is signed. This page covers three versions of that record.

**Tax and accounting workpapers.** For each client each year: the source records, a schedule for each account, the preparer's treatment, the manager's queries, the answers, the tax return as filed, and sometimes a later change by the tax office.

**Audit files.** The risk assessment, the samples tested, the exceptions found, the manager's and partner's review notes with how each was cleared, the adjustments proposed and waived, and the signed opinion.

**Audits of self-managed super funds.** In Australia a family can run its own small pension fund, with the members as trustees. Each fund must be audited every year by a registered auditor, who gives one opinion on the accounts and another on whether the fund obeyed the pension law. Where a breach meets set tests, the auditor must report it to the tax office.

An illustration, not a real file: a fund's accountant sends the year's accounts and documents to the auditor. The auditor's checklist flags a $40,000 transfer to a member's personal bank account. The auditor asks whether it was a pension payment or a loan. The accountant replies that the member was short of cash and repaid it four months later. The auditor treats it as a loan to a member, applies the tax office's reporting tests, qualifies the compliance opinion, reports the breach as already put right, and writes to the trustees. The final check is a rule whose answer the regulator defined.
Why it might matter for training AI
Vendors' pages show labs asking for accounting and tax firms' records and for expert judgement with reasons. A reviewer's query and the correction that follows is that.

The clearest sign of value is not a purchase. An investment group backed by OpenAI owns accounting firms in the United States and raised US$2 billion in 2026 [techcrunch-2026]. An account of its tax product says the product keeps what the software proposed, what the accountant changed and what went into the filed return [montana]. That is the review record, captured inside firms the group owns, with no data bought from anyone.
No purchase of pension fund audit files by a lab or a vendor was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

There were about 672,805 [ato-mar-2026] self-managed funds in March 2026. One audit software product says it keeps review points, red flags and queries against each line and can export them with the audit file [cloudoffis].
Who may share is set by professional rules:

items: The Australian auditing guidance on working papers says they are the auditor's property, and that the client's consent is needed before the auditor gives anyone else access unless the law requires it [gs011].

The accountants' ethics code goes beyond disclosure. It says a member must not use confidential client information for the advantage of the member, the firm or a third party, unless the client has authorised it [apes110]. Whether removing names takes a file outside that rule was not established.
The Tax Practitioners Board's code says a tax agent must not disclose a client's affairs to a third party without the client's permission or a legal duty [tpb].

The software companies cannot be the route. Xero's developer terms say data drawn through its developer platform must not be used to train or fine-tune AI models [xero-terms]. MYOB's developer terms contain a similar bar and extend it to pooled or shared datasets [myob-terms]. Files a firm exports from its own system are a different matter.

blocks.text: Who is already there
In the United States, the OpenAI-backed group described above. Nothing like it was found in Australia.
Australian makers of fund audit software describe automated checks and AI flags in their products [cloudoffis] [evolv] [asf]. None says it trains models on client files or sells data.
For Australian pension fund audit files, no buyer, public test or research paper was found.
What would have to be stripped

These files are full of identified people: names, addresses, tax file numbers, bank accounts, income, fund balances and sometimes health details. All of it would have to go, and the amounts would have to be altered.
What stands in the way

items: Every file needs the client's authority. For a pension fund the client is the trustees, whom the auditor usually reaches only through the fund's accountant.
The rules are Australian. Whether a lab would pay for work under one country's pension and tax law is unanswered.
Auditors of these funds are closely watched by the tax office, and a seller who gets this wrong risks professional discipline.
A group that owns firms can capture the same record from the inside.

blocks.text: The record
This page covers two records kept by lenders to small and mid-sized businesses.

**The credit file.** For a business loan: the application and accounts, the analyst's credit memo (a written case for lending that covers the business, its cash flow, the security, the risks, the proposed terms and a risk grade), the approval and its conditions, the yearly review notes, and any waivers. If the loan goes bad, the file continues with demand letters, a rescue deal or the appointment of a receiver, the sale of the security and the final loss.

**The invoice-finance ledger.** A business raises cash against its unpaid invoices. The financier records each invoice offered, any check made with the customer who owes the money, the cash advanced, and then what happened: paid in full, paid short, disputed, or found to be fake.

An illustration, not a real file: a lender advances $400,000 to a labour-hire firm against its invoices. The memo notes that a handful of customers owe most of the money, sets a limit and takes a guarantee from the director. Some months later a checking call finds one customer disputing $100,000, and the lender stops funding that customer's invoices. Then the largest customer collapses and the lender appoints a receiver over its client. Within two years it has recovered 60 cents in the dollar. The last step follows a real pattern: the administrators' report on one failed Australian financier records its lender appointing receivers over invoice-finance clients [bizpay-report].
The answer comes quickly for an invoice and slowly for a loan.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for finance work, for expert judgement with reasons, and for real records where the steps are visible. A memo followed by the loan's actual result offers judgement with an outcome attached.
No purchase of such records by a lab or a vendor was found. Where labs want a banker's reasoning, the evidence is that they pay experts to write it fresh.
Who holds it and who may share it

Lenders hold their own files. The dossier found several Australian non-bank business lenders that failed or sold books in recent years. One, liquidated in 2023, had a loan pool valued at $2.56 million [herald-funda] and by a press account had assessed loans within a day. Another entered administration the same year with a loan book of about 150 [bizpay-report] clients, carried at $2.7 million [bizpay-report], and was later sold through a deed with its creditors [bizpay-deed]. A listed company sold its invoice-finance portfolio for $2 million [spenda-grapple] in 2025. One working financier has told investors it is merging three [earlypay-fy25] old loan systems into one.
Invoice finance is sizeable. An industry yearbook estimates about A$95 billion [bcr-2026] of invoices were financed in Australia in 2025.

On a sale of a loan book the buyer takes the debts and, in the wording of one such deed, the benefit of the contracts [bizpay-deed]. In an insolvency the secured lender's receiver usually controls the loan book and the liquidator the company's records.

Controlling a file is not the same as a right to reuse it. Borrowers' information is held in confidence. For credit-bureau reports inside a file, the credit-reporting part of the Privacy Act restricts use and disclosure to listed purposes [privacy-act]; only its headings and definitions were read, so what those sections permit was not established. Whether a liquidator may sell copies of a failed lender's files with names removed was also not established.
Who is already there

One American processor of loan applications says it handles roughly 750,000 [ocrolus] a month and sells credit signals built on the resulting dataset inside its own product. That is bank statements, not memos or recoveries.

A maker of memo-drafting software for banks advertises a contractual promise that neither it nor its suppliers may use bank or borrower data to train or improve foundation models [aloan]. Lenders are starting to demand that clause.

A research company sells a map of who lends to whom in the United States, built from more than 40 million [applied-econ] archived loan documents covering 1.8 million [applied-econ] firms. Nothing suggests it contains credit memos.
No seller, dataset or public test was found for the whole file from memo to recovery.
What would have to be stripped

A company borrower is not a person, but small-business files are full of people: directors, guarantors, sole traders, their tax returns, home addresses and the properties pledged. Credit-bureau reports and anything derived from them would have to come out. So would the names of the customers on an invoice ledger, which are businesses with their own claims to confidentiality.
What stands in the way

items: The rich file is not where the failures are. Lenders that fail tend to be newer firms that decide by algorithm in a day, so a written memo and yearly reviews may barely exist. This is an inference from how fast those lenders said they assessed loans.
Confidence and credit-reporting law fence the most useful parts, and lenders increasingly write a ban on training into their contracts.
No buyer has been shown for records that carry real outcomes.
Australian volumes from any one failed lender are small.
Processors and software platforms already capture the value where it exists.

blocks.text: The record

A chargeback is a cardholder asking their own bank, the issuer, to reverse a card payment. The merchant may contest it by sending an evidence pack through its bank or payment processor, the acquirer. A pack holds the order record, the delivery scan, device and network details, emails with the customer, the refund policy and a short letter of rebuttal. The issuer decides. Either side can then push the matter up to the card scheme, Visa or Mastercard, for a final ruling.
A worked example. The purchase is invented; the fee and time limits are from two Australian acquirers' merchant guides.

items: A customer buys a jacket online from a Melbourne shop.
Some weeks later the customer tells their bank the jacket never arrived. The bank raises a chargeback with a reason code.

The shop's acquirer debits the purchase price and, at one large bank, a fee of A$25 [nab-guide]. One acquirer gives the shop 7 days [tyro-guide] to answer. The bank allows up to 30 days [nab-guide] on a Visa card and 45 days [nab-guide] on a Mastercard.
The shop sends its pack: the order confirmation, the courier's proof of delivery, and a chat in which the customer asked about sizing after the delivery date.
The issuer accepts or pushes back.
The shop gets its money back, or does not.

blocks.text: The record is the claim, the reason code, the pack, and a win or loss in money a month or more later. Whether issuers give merchants written reasons was not established.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for practice tasks with a check that is hard to game. Here an outside party pays real money or does not. The usable form would be a practice setting in which a system gathers the evidence from order, shipping and support records, builds a pack, and is scored against what actually happened.
The result is noisy. A pack that lost may have been a good pack.
No purchase of this record by a lab or a vendor was found. The companies that value it collect it as a by-product of their own service.
Who holds it and who may share it

Merchants hold their own packs. Acquirers, processors, dispute companies and the card schemes hold far more. Visa says it processed 106 million [visa-2026] disputes in 2025. A research firm's summary estimates 261 million [datos-2025] chargebacks worldwide that year and puts the Asia-Pacific dispute rate lowest of any region, at 0.007% [datos-2025] of card transactions against 0.051% [datos-2025] in North America.
Can a merchant license its own packs? The schemes' published rules say no, for anything that still contains transaction or cardholder information.

items: Mastercard's rules say a merchant must not sell, provide or in any way disclose account or transaction data, or personal information about a cardholder, to anyone other than its acquirer, the acquirer's service provider, Mastercard, or a government with a valid demand. The ban extends to database files and other media created as a result of a transaction [mc-rules].

Visa's rules let an acquirer or merchant disclose transaction information to third parties, without the issuer's and Visa's consent, only for three purposes: a loyalty programme, fraud control, and completing the original sale [visa-rules].

blocks.text: These rules reach the merchant through its acquirer's contract; one Australian acquirer's terms require compliance with scheme rules [tyro-terms].
Whether a pack with all identifying detail removed is still "transaction data" under the Mastercard rule is untested.
Who is already there

Justt says it serves more than 250 [justt] enterprise merchants. Chargeflow says it learns from millions of past cases [chargeflow]. Stripe builds packs for its merchants from its own data and theirs and charges only on a win [stripe-smart].
Visa itself announced AI dispute products in 2026, among them one that drafts the merchant's reply and scores its chance of winning [visa-2026].
A free practice setting for chargebacks exists, with a scripted issuer; its cases are made up [chargebackops].

One real Australian set has reached researchers. A payments company gave academics 126,184 [novatti-study] charged-back transactions with customer details, card identifiers and network addresses removed; the fraud rate was 0.31% [novatti-study].
What would have to be stripped
Almost everything. A pack is personal information from end to end: name, addresses, email, phone, device details, purchase history, support chat and sometimes photographs of identity documents.
What stands in the way

items: Both schemes' rules bar a merchant from selling or disclosing transaction data.
Visa, Stripe and the dispute companies already train on the record at a scale no outsider can match.
A stripped pack loses most of what made it useful.
The result is noisy and the task short, and a free made-up alternative exists.
No lab has been shown to buy this kind of record.

blocks.text: The record
A quantity surveyor is the professional who measures and prices building work. This page covers three linked records that set a cost forecast against what the work finally cost.

**The lender's surveyor's reports.** A bank or private lender funding a development hires its own quantity surveyor. Before the loan the surveyor reports on whether the building contract price is enough and whether approvals and insurance are in place. Then, each month, the surveyor reviews the builder's claim for payment. The profession's guidance lists what that report holds, including the adjusted contract sum, the value of work completed, the current valuation, progress against the programme and a certificate of the cost to complete [nziqs-2019]. The lender releases that month's money on the certificate.
**Cost plan against final account.** The developer's surveyor prices the design at each stage, then administers the contract. The final account is what the building cost after all changes.

**A civil contractor's bid against actual cost.** A road or pipeline builder prices a tender line by line in estimating software, then tracks actual labour, machinery and materials against the same cost codes.

An illustration, not a real file: a lender funds a $40 million apartment project with a $30 million building contract. In one month the builder claims $3 million. The lender's surveyor walks the site, values the work done at $2.5 million, refuses cladding that is still off site, and certifies $2.5 million. Some months later, changes to the work have used up most of the allowance for surprises, and the surveyor reports that the cost to finish now exceeds the money left in the loan. The lender asks the developer to put in more of its own. The building is finished for $32 million, against a tender-stage cost plan of $29 million.
Each month is a judgement followed by a number that later proves right or wrong.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for construction records, among them estimates and change orders, and for tasks with a check that is hard to game. Cost plans and bids give one answer per project, years later. The lender's reports give a run of certified steps on each.

No purchase of such records by a lab or a vendor was found. The sign of value is that product companies build on them: one American lending-software firm says its payment-review product draws on more than $3 trillion [built-lenders] of real estate finance data.
Who holds it and who may share it

**Lender's reports.** Quantity-surveying firms, banks and private lenders hold them. The guidance note read, a New Zealand adaptation of the Australian one, says reports go only to the lender that appointed the surveyor unless that lender releases them in writing, and should not be passed on without the authority of both surveyor and lender [nziqs-2019]. So two consents are needed, and in practice a third, because the report describes the borrower's project and its builder. The Australian original was not read.

**Cost plans.** The surveying firm holds the working files. Its client owns the project's commercial information. No firm's engagement terms were found. One slice is public: large projects assessed by the state in New South Wales need a cost report from a certified surveyor on a standard form, and these are published [nsw-edc]. One such report, for a Sydney project, gives an estimate of A$108,589,952 [wt-edc] before tax. This is the estimate only. No final account is published.
**Civil bids.** The contractor owns both ends and can consent alone.

**Software platforms.** Procore's customer agreement says customer data remains owned exclusively by the customer, while Procore may compile aggregated data [procore-ssa]. A third-party summary of Procore's developer terms says makers of commercial apps may not use data drawn through its connections to train or test AI systems [procore-summary]; Procore's own page was not opened. Autodesk's terms say a customer's content stays the customer's and that Autodesk uses it in connection with providing and improving its products [autodesk-terms].
Who is already there

In the United States, a lending-software company launched an AI product in 2025 that reviews builders' payment claims for lenders. It says the product handles thousands of claims a month and can review one in as few as three [built-draw] minutes.
A British cost service sells benchmarks drawn from 21,000 [bcis] projects. It sells averages and cost breakdowns, not the stage-by-stage trail.
No Australian firm was found selling, or training on, cost plans paired with final accounts.
What would have to be stripped

There is little personal information: the names of consultants and site staff, and signed declarations by the builder's officers. The sensitive content is commercial: the borrower's loan terms, the builder's margins and rates, and the lender's view of the credit.
What stands in the way

items: Lender's reports need the lender's and the surveyor's consent, and in practice the borrower's. One refusal ends it.
No lab has been shown to buy an estimate paired with the actual cost.
An American company already holds the equivalent record at a scale that makes an Australian sample look small.
A report that shows a surveyor missed a cost overrun is evidence against that firm. Firms also treat their archives as an edge.
Each project yields one final answer, and it arrives late.

This page covers three Australian records in which an outside party rules on building work. They earn different verdicts, given separately in the box.

**Apartment bond inspection reports (New South Wales).** The state government's page on the scheme says the developer of a new apartment building lodges a bond equal to 2% [nsw-bond] of the contract price. An independent inspector then reports twice on a set form. The interim report, due 15 to 18 months [nsw-bond] after the building may be occupied, lists defective work. The final report, by the same inspector, says for each listed defect whether it was fixed, and may not add new ones [nsw-bond]. The cost of what remains is paid from the bond.

**Payment adjudications.** Every state has a law that speeds up payment in the building trade. A subcontractor serves a payment claim. The head contractor replies with a schedule saying what it will pay and why not the rest. If they disagree, an adjudicator gives a written decision with reasons and a dollar figure within days.
**Collapsed builders' files.** When a builder is liquidated, its project files pass to the liquidator's control: contracts, claims, changes to the work, queries, programmes, defect lists and email.

A worked example for adjudication, using official New South Wales averages; the builder's offer is invented. A waterproofing subcontractor claims A$617,276 [nsw-sop-2025], the average claim in the state for one quarter of 2025. The builder's schedule offers far less, citing defects and changes it never approved. An adjudicator, appointed through an approved body, reads both sides and awards A$284,105 [nsw-sop-2025], the average award that quarter.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for construction records, for legal case files, and for expert judgement with reasons. Adjudication has the best shape: a claim and a reply go in, and a reasoned figure for each item comes out in days. The bond reports give an expert's list of defects and then a ruling on each. A collapsed builder's files are raw company records of the kind data brokers buy.
No purchase of any of the three by a lab was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**Bond reports.** The scheme's page says each approved report goes to the state's building regulator, the building's owners and the developer, and that the inspector gives the builder a copy [nsw-bond-3]. The government's copy is not published. How many are lodged a year was not found. The Act itself was not opened, and who owns copyright in a report was not established.
**Adjudications.** The states differ.

items: Queensland publishes adjudication decisions on the regulator's website, and its application form says the Act requires it [qbcc-registry]. In the first half of 2025 it released 106 [qbcc-h1-2025] decisions, from 175 [qbcc-h1-2025] valid applications worth A$193,702,366 [qbcc-h1-2025]; A$48,563,395 [qbcc-h1-2025] was awarded.

New South Wales does not publish them. In 2024-25 there were 990 [nsw-sop-2025] applications and 493 [nsw-sop-2025] decisions released to the parties, with A$547,219,189 [nsw-sop-2025] claimed and A$170,203,408 [nsw-sop-2025] awarded. The parties and the appointing bodies hold them.
Victoria publishes a spreadsheet with a row for each application under an open licence, with amounts and dates but no reasons [vic-data].

blocks.text: The claim, the schedule and the two sides' submissions are published nowhere. They belong to the parties.

**Collapsed builders.** Construction leads the country's insolvencies: 898 [asic-34] construction companies entered external administration in one quarter of 2024. The files are the company's, under the liquidator's control. Procore's customer agreement says customer data stays owned exclusively by the customer [procore-ssa]. A third-party summary of Procore's developer terms says app makers may not bulk-export or train on data drawn through its connections [procore-summary]; Procore's own page was not opened.
Who is already there
A legal research product offers more than 7,300 [sopal] Queensland adjudication decisions in full text, with search by adjudicator, outcome and amount, and drafting help.
Construction software platforms are building AI on their own customers' live projects [enr-2026].
Brokers buy the data of closed companies elsewhere. None was found working with Australian liquidators.
What would have to be stripped

items: Bond reports: unit numbers, occupants' names and photographs inside homes. A report also reveals a building's faults, which bears on what owners can sell for.
Adjudications: mostly companies, with some sole traders and named people. Unpublished decisions are confidential to the parties.
Collapsed builders: the most. Employee records, subcontractors' bank details, and home-owner customers' details and emails.

blocks.text: Whether Australian copyright law allows text to be mined without a licence was not established.
What stands in the way

items: Collapsed builders: a liquidator may judge that privacy and other parties' confidentiality outweigh a modest recovery for creditors, and platform access can lapse before anything is exported.
Adjudications: the valuable half, the claim and the schedule, is unpublished. Rebuilding the inputs from the published reasons leaks the answer. The public half is already a product.
Bond reports: one state, modest numbers, private, and consent building by building.
No lab has been shown to buy any of the three.

When old industrial land is redeveloped, an environmental consultant investigates it and writes a chain of reports: a study of the site's history, a detailed investigation that tests soil and groundwater against health limits, a plan for the clean-up, and a final report with test results from after the clean-up.

In Victoria and New South Wales a second expert, accredited by the state's environment regulator, then reviews that work and signs a formal statement on whether the land is fit for its proposed use. In Victoria a lighter first step screens out sites that do not need a full audit.
The record is the consultant's reports with their laboratory tables, the auditor's review and reasons, and a ruling: fit, fit with conditions, or not fit.

A real example, from a statement the New South Wales regulator hosts in public. The site is one lot of a former lead and zinc smelter near Newcastle. Several consultancies had investigated and cleaned it up over the years, and earlier audit statements for the smelter land go back to 2004 [gn416]. A site auditor at another firm reviewed the reports and issued a statement with an audit report dated 2018 [gn416]. The statement records the auditor's conclusion on fitness for the stated use, with any conditions, such as a plan for continuing management.

The numbers are on the Victorian side. The regulator's register there was queried on 12 October 2026 and returned 5,451 [vic-wfs] audit records. Nearly all of these carried a link to documents, and most a link to appendices. No individual Victorian report was opened, so what the appendices hold is inferred.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for expert judgement with reasons and for private tests. Here one accountable expert rules on another's long technical work, across several documents, with laboratory figures that give a second, numerical check. No vendor's or lab's page names environmental work; the fit is inferred.
No purchase of this record by a lab or a vendor was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**Victoria publishes the reports.** The regulator's public register lists screening and audit reports submitted since 1991, each with the report attached [vic-register]. Its guidance says the auditor must give the statement and report to the regulator within 5 [vic-audits] business days of finishing, and to the client and the planning authority. The register shows completed audits running at a couple of hundred a year [vic-wfs].

Public to read is not the same as free to reuse. The register's index is an open government dataset under a Creative Commons attribution licence [vic-data]. The regulator's copyright page licenses its own material the same way but excludes content supplied by third parties, and warns that their permission may be needed [vic-copyright]. The audit reports are written by private auditors and consultants.

**New South Wales receives statements, not usually reports.** The regulator's page says that for audits required by law the auditor must send the statement to it and to the local council [nsw-scheme]. Full reports reach the public mostly as attachments to planning applications. That may change: minutes of a 2025 meeting between the regulator and auditors record a proposal that auditors routinely lodge full reports as well [nsw-minutes]. Whether it was adopted was not established.
Whether consultants and auditors keep copyright in their reports was not checked against any firm's terms.
Who is already there

Several American software companies draft or read environmental site reports for consultancies and lenders. One states that customer data never trains its models [remedient]. All work on one customer's files at a time. None was found holding reports from many firms, a public test, or anything that pairs a consultant's work with an independent auditor's ruling.
The New South Wales regulator told auditors in 2025 that it had no formal policy on AI and would form a working group [nsw-minutes].
No dataset, test or paper using the Victorian register was found.
What would have to be stripped
Little. The reports name owners, auditors and consultants, and now and then neighbours and home addresses. The site's address is part of the record and already public.
What stands in the way

items: No buyer has been identified.

The report texts belong to third parties. Reading public reports is one thing; copying thousands into something sold for training is another. Whether Australian copyright law has an exception for this was not established.

The outcomes vary little. The public record shows the signed-off state, and sites that fail tend to be cleaned further until they pass. The telling content is the conditions and the reasons, not the yes or no.
The reports are long scanned documents with laboratory tables, so extracting them is real work.
The richest material, the auditor's comments on the consultant's drafts, is on no register.

A mine predicts what is in the ground several times, each time in finer detail. The resource model divides the rock into blocks and estimates the metal content, or grade, of each from widely spaced drill holes. The grade-control model re-estimates the same ground from closely spaced samples, days before it is dug. The dig plan then marks each patch as ore, low-grade or waste. Ore goes to the mill and waste to the dump.
The mill weighs and tests what actually arrives. Reconciliation is the monthly comparison of predicted tonnes, grade and metal against what the mill measured.

An illustration, not a real file: a geologist tests the samples from one level of a pit, estimates the grade of each block, and draws the line between ore and waste. The surveyor marks it on the ground and the trucks follow it. Over the month the mill processes a blend from several parts of the pit. At month end the reconciliation sheet shows that the mill received a tenth less metal than grade control predicted. Someone investigates why, and changes the estimating settings.

One real price exists, for mine data of a different kind. In 2023 a minerals explorer that uses AI paid another explorer US$175,000 [aem-2023] for test results, 13 [aem-2023] drill holes and airborne surveys covering ground the buyer itself held. That was a neighbour buying information about its own land, not a purchase of training data.
Why it might matter for training AI
This is a prediction followed by a physical measurement, the kind of check that is hard to argue with.

The check is coarser than it looks. The mill measures a month's blended feed, often after the rock has sat in stockpiles. It does not say which block or which call was wrong. A mining software company's own case study describes stockpile grades being updated by hand in a spreadsheet at month end [datamine].
No lab, vendor or broker was found naming mining, and no purchase of this record was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

The mining company or joint venture owns the record. The software companies only process it, and say so. One geology software maker's terms state that customer data remains the customer's and will be copied only as needed to provide the service [seequent-terms]. Another's statement on its AI feature says each training run uses only that user's own data and that the company keeps no copy [micromine-ai]. So no software company can license it, and some have promised in public not to pool it.

What the law makes public in Western Australia is exploration reports only. The state mines department's summary says explorers must file yearly reports and that the department may release them after five [wamex] years, subject to objections. Its archive holds over 120,000 [wamex-portal] reports, more than 105,000 [wamex-portal] of them public, and a database of more than 2 million [wamex] drill holes. None of it is grade control, dig plans or mill results. The regulation itself was not read.

Mines do change hands through insolvency. At a gold operation that entered administration in 2026, trade press reported about 40% [matsa] unplanned dilution, meaning waste mixed into the ore: a live case of ore-or-waste calls failing against production. In such cases the data is part of the secured asset and goes with the mine to its buyer, who needs it to restart.
Who is already there
Software for the reconciliation task exists and is sold as software, with no data business attached [datamine] [intellisense].

One company builds machine-learning models for grade control and reconciliation inside each customer's site, using that site's existing data. It claims 32 to 55% [stratum-tech] lower deviation in reconciliation.

AI-led explorers buy or trade for exploration data: the purchase above and an alliance giving one explorer access to a large miner's exploration databases [bhp-kobold]. All of it is exploration, none reconciliation.
Public real data is scarce. One open set from a Brazilian processing plant has 737,453 [frothiq] rows and covers the plant side only.
No dataset, public test or seller of this record was found.
What would have to be stripped

Almost no personal information: a geologist's initials on a log. The sensitive content is commercial. Grade and reconciliation results can move a listed company's share price. Joint-venture partners have confidentiality terms. Map layers that record native title and heritage sites would have to come out, and locations would have to be shifted and grades rescaled to hide the mine.
What stands in the way

items: No buyer was found outside mining-AI companies, and their customers hand them the data.
The check is monthly and blended. At most mines the truth about a single block does not exist.
The owner is the only party who can license it and has market reasons to refuse.
When a mine is sold out of insolvency, the data follows the mine.

A refinery, smelter, mill or power station is run from a control room. Each control loop has a target the operator types in (the setpoint), a sensor reading, an output such as a valve position, and a mode: manual, automatic, or handed to a more advanced controller. A database called a historian stores all of these every few seconds or minutes, for many thousands of measuring points, for decades. A laboratory system stores tests of product quality every few hours. The control system's event journal records who changed what, along with alarms. Shift logs hold the operator's reasons in plain words.
This page covers two forms of the record: the operator's changes set against later product quality, at any plant, and the whole control-room history of a plant that has closed.

An illustration, not a real file: in the small hours, an operator at an alumina refinery sees the temperature of the process liquid drifting. The operator takes the loop into manual and raises the steam target by a few percent. The reading follows over the next half hour and an alarm clears. The morning laboratory sample shows the product back within its limits. The shift log reads "feed change, raised steam".

One company that builds AI controllers publishes what it needs, which gives real numbers for the shape. It asks for every part of each main loop to be recorded, at one-minute [imubit-data] intervals, with at least 200 [imubit-data] laboratory samples, and says its models are usually trained on 2 to 5 [imubit-data] years of history.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for manufacturing records and for real work where the steps are visible, though most of those voices are middlemen. One marketplace's summary for buyers lists production telemetry among the data on offer [privara].

A plant's behaviour is particular to that plant. The history of a closed plant can teach general physics and operator habits, but nobody will run a controller on a demolished unit. That narrows the likely buyer to builders of general models.
No purchase of historian data by a lab was found, and no completed broker sale. Every process-AI company found trains inside a customer's contract on that customer's own data.
Who holds it and who may share it

The plant's owner owns the data. The historian's maker licenses only the software. The most common historian's published terms describe the licence as personal and non-transferable [aveva-pi]. They require the maker's written consent before the software is moved or the licence assigned, and require use to end when a subscription expires [osisoft-licence]. They also say that sharing data through the software as part of a business model or commercial engagement needs a separate agreement with the maker [osisoft-usage]. Whether exporting to plain files for a data licence falls under that clause was not established.
The practical point is one of timing. The owner would have to export the data while its licence is live. That deadline comes before demolition.
Australian closures, as checked:

items: An alumina refinery in Western Australia stopped production in 2024, and its owner announced permanent closure in 2025. The owner said demolition and clean-up would begin in 2026 and run for six [alcoa-2025] years. The plant's capacity was 2.2 million [alcoa-2025] tonnes a year. The owner is solvent.
A coal power station in New South Wales was due to close in 2023, by its owner's announcement that January [agl-2023]; early demolition was under way in 2025 [hunternet].
A Victorian oil refinery's decommissioning was completed in 2023 [liberty].
A Victorian paper mill sometimes described as closed is still operating [opal].

blocks.text: Whether any of these owners archived its historian was not established.
Who is already there

Brokers already list this record. One works on commission and names historians and plant control systems among what it takes from owners [datanexx]. One runs an anonymous marketplace that lists production telemetry and names frontier AI labs as buyers [privara]. A third, by a press account, sources operating data from distressed companies and bankruptcies [petrarch-article]. None shows a completed sale of historian data.

The process-AI companies train plant by plant. One describes a model built for each plant from that customer's own historian and laboratory data [imubit-fpm]. Another says data stays with the customer [intellisense].
Nobody was found working with closed Australian plants.
What would have to be stripped

Operators' log-in names in the event journal and names in shift logs are ordinary employee information and would be removed or replaced. The commercial sensitivities are the confidentiality of whoever licensed the process design, customers' names in laboratory records, and the details of sister plants that still run the same process.
What stands in the way

items: No buyer for historian data has been shown anywhere.
An owner with sister plants still running has a reason to refuse.
The software licence may lapse, or the servers be scrapped, before anything is exported.
Without the list that says what each measuring point physically is, and without the event journal, the archive is close to unusable.
The historian maker's clause on commercial data sharing.

title: Process plants: operators' control changes and the control-room history of closed plants

blocks.text: The record
Three records sit on this page, and they do not share a verdict.

**Programs against inspection.** A job shop cuts metal parts from drawings its customers supply. Each job leaves behind the drawing, the program that steers the cutting machine, a set-up sheet saying how the part was held and which tools were used, and an inspection report from a measuring machine that marks every dimension as inside or outside its allowed range. When a first part fails and the program is changed until a part passes, the file holds an attempt, a measured failure and a fix.
**Quote against actual.** Before taking the job the shop estimated its hours. Afterwards its job card shows the hours and the scrap that really resulted.

**Design changes against the failure behind them.** A manufacturer that owns a product keeps a formal log of each design change and the reason given. Tied to the fault report that prompted it, an entry reads as failure, diagnosis, change, and whether the change held.

An illustration, not a real file: a shop quotes forty aluminium housings at two hours of set-up and twenty minutes a part. The first finished part fails inspection because one bore is slightly too tight. The programmer alters the last cut and swaps a tool, and the next part passes. The job card closes at five hours of set-up, twenty-five minutes a part, and three parts scrapped.
Why it might matter for training AI
Vendors' pages show labs asking for real work with a check that cannot be argued with, and for design and manufacturing records. A measuring machine's verdict on a part is that kind of check.

No sale of any of the three records to a lab or a data vendor was found. The company best placed to want them went the other way: CloudNC, which sells software that writes cutting programs, built its own factory to make its own data and says it does not train on what customers put in [mms].
Who holds it and who may share it
The shop holds the first two records. Whether it may share them turns on its customers' purchase terms, and the published ones read alike.

items: Mattel's terms say drawings, specifications, tooling and technical information that it supplies or pays for stay its property and may be used only to fill its orders [mattel].

Textron's terms say the same of drawings and data. They add that anything the supplier devises while doing the work, or derives from the buyer's confidential information, becomes the buyer's [textron].

blocks.text: Under terms like these the cutting program may belong to the customer as well, since it is worked out from the drawing. No court decision on that point was found. What the shop plainly owns is its estimate, its hours and its scrap count, and those say little once the shape of the part is taken away.

The third record is different. The manufacturer owns its own designs and its own change log. Whether an insolvency administrator can sell such a log free of suppliers' confidentiality terms was not established.

CloudNC advertises a government-only cloud option for export-controlled customers [cloudnc], a sign that part data for defence work is treated as controlled. The export rules themselves were not opened for this dossier.
Who is already there

items: **CloudNC** trains on simulated parts and its own factory. Its support page says many firms are unwilling to see their parts teach another company's AI [cloudnc-support].

**Privara** lists anonymised operating data from industrial equipment for sale to buyers that it says include frontier AI labs [privara]. These are machine readings, not programs with drawings, and no sale is shown.

**DataNexx** lists inspection, quality and change-control systems among the sources it will broker, on commission, and says on the same page that owning data is not the same as having permission to license it [datanexx].
**Petrarch** is reported to buy operating data out of bankruptcies, which is the nearest thing to the third record [petrarch].

blocks.text: Nobody was found selling design changes linked to the failures behind them.
What would have to be stripped

There is little personal information: operators' names on job cards and inspectors' stamps. The sensitive content is the customer's design. Removing the drawing removes the difficulty and most of the worth.
What stands in the way

items: The drawing is the customer's, and on the usual purchase terms so may be the program made from it. The shop holds files it cannot license.
Any file tied to defence work is likely to be controlled, and cannot be mixed in with the rest.
For design change logs, supply is thin and brokers of bankrupt companies' data are already active.

title: Machine-shop job records and design change histories

blocks.text: The record
Four records sit on this page. Each is a piece of technical work followed by a plain result, and each gets its own verdict.

**Help-desk tickets with the recorded fix.** A managed service provider looks after small businesses' computers. When a user reports a fault, a technician takes remote control of the machine, fixes it and writes a note. The result is whether the ticket reopened in the following days. If recording was on, a video of the screen exists too.

**Mainframe changes against the overnight run.** A bank alters a program written in COBOL, an old business language. The package for the change contains the code before and after, with the test evidence. The result is whether the overnight batch finished or stopped with an error code.

**Factory controller edits against downtime.** An engineer changes the logic in the small industrial computer that runs a machine, and change-management software keeps every version. The result, lost production before and after, sits in a separate system.
**Outage timelines.** Alerts, charts, chat, commands and the written review of a software outage, in order, wrong turns included.

An illustration, not a real file: at nine in the morning a user reports that the email program will not open. A technician connects ten minutes later, tries a repair that fails, finds a damaged add-in, removes it, checks with the user and closes the ticket by half past nine. It does not reopen in the next two weeks.
Why it might matter for training AI
Vendors' pages show labs asking for long tasks with recovery from failure, and for checks that need no human opinion. All four records have that form.

The help-desk record has something the others lack: a lab has moved towards its holders. In December 2025 OpenAI became a part-owner of Thrive Holdings. A trade publication reported that the deal gives OpenAI access to 7 service providers bought by a Thrive company, and quoted an Omdia analyst saying OpenAI would be able to train on their IT services data [channeldive]. That is a lab buying into the holders. It is not a purchase of a dataset, and no sale of tickets with sessions was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**Help-desk sessions** have three layers. The ticket text and the technician's note are the provider's. What appears on the user's screen is the client's: ConnectWise's master agreement says the client alone owns client data [connectwise], and NinjaOne's data-processing agreement says customer data stays the customer's property [ninjaone-dpa]. The third layer is the maker of the remote-access tool. NinjaOne's agreement of June 2026 says it may use aggregated or anonymised data to develop and train its products and its AI models [ninjaone-dpa]. An earlier version was read only in part, so when that wording arrived was not established. Whether session recording is usually switched on was not established.
**Mainframe changes** belong to the bank, insurer or government that runs the system.

**Controller histories** belong to the plant owner, with copies at the firms that built or fitted the machines. A reseller says one long-used product for storing these histories, AutoSave, reaches the end of its supported life in 2026 [becolve], so its users are moving their histories or leaving them behind.
Who is already there
For help-desk work, OpenAI through Thrive, and the tool makers through their terms. No public test built from real help-desk sessions was found.

For mainframes, a software company, Factory, published a test of old-code tasks in 2026, built from constructed tasks and not real change packages. By its account COBOL accounts for 31 of the 44 tasks that defeated every model [legacy-bench].
For factory controllers, research projects only. Whether the firms that store customers' histories train on them was not confirmed either way.

For outages, the field is crowded with published tests, nearly all made by injecting faults into demonstration systems. A paper comparing them says injected faults are cleaner than real ones, which often have several causes at once [aiops-compare].
What would have to be stripped

Help-desk recordings are the heaviest case: they show names, email, documents, the client's own customers and passwords as they are typed. Mainframe test files often contain real customer records, and outage logs contain secrets. Controller code holds no personal data. The Australian privacy and workplace-recording rules were not opened for this dossier.
What stands in the way

items: The client owns what is on the screen, and consent has to be gathered client by client.
A lab-backed buyer of providers and the tool makers already sit upstream of every independent provider.
Mainframe change packages cannot be reached from outside the firm doing the work.
Controller histories carry no result of their own; downtime must be joined in, site by site.
Tests of outage handling are plentiful, and the real evidence stays inside live companies.

title: IT operations work that either held or did not

blocks.text: The record

A proficiency test is an exam that laboratories sit by post. The scheme's operator sends an identical sample, image or written case to all the labs enrolled, and each reports what it finds. The operator, which knows the right answer in advance, scores the labs and tells each how it compared with the rest. The record is the item, its true answer, all the answers given and the scores.

Most rounds are measurements, such as the sugar level in a vial, where a machine gives the answer; those are of no use to a language or image model. The rest are interpretive: reading a blood film, diagnosing from a slide, answering a written case, comparing bullets. A trained person answers these, and they are the subject here.

A worked example from the Australian operator's own conference poster. In its 2025 chemical pathology case-study programme the operator sent out 3 written cases with 5 questions each to 94 enrolled participants [rcpaqap-poster]. They returned 470 answers [rcpaqap-poster], which is 94 people answering 5 questions. An expert committee held the target answers. Staff summarised the anonymous answers with a general AI assistant, the committee edited the result, and reports went out in 28 to 63 days where they had taken 80 to 163 [rcpaqap-poster]. One case therefore yields its text, the target answers, a professional answer from nearly every participant on each question, and the committee's commentary.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for private tests that no model has seen, refreshed often, with a human baseline. Each year's rounds are new, are not published, and arrive with many professionals' answers to every item.

This is a test set and not training material: an item has one answer and no working. No purchase of such a set by a lab or a vendor was found. The nearest thing found is something offered and not something sold: an animal-imaging company, Sage, advertises scoring a customer's model against a sealed set it never licenses for training [sage].
Who holds it and who may share it

**Australia.** The medical schemes are run by RCPAQAP, a company belonging to the pathologists' Royal College. Its participation guidelines say its material may not be reproduced without written permission, and name a financial incentive to others as a ground on which permission may be refused [rcpaqap-guidelines]. The operator owns the items, the answers and the reports. A lab owns only its own answer.
**United States.** The College of American Pathologists is the main operator. Its terms treat non-public information about its products, data and customers as confidential [cap-terms].

**United Kingdom.** UK NEQAS is a group of schemes hosted in the health service. One of them says participant information is handled under the confidentiality terms of the international standard for such schemes [ukneqas]. Its full clause on reuse was not read.
**Outside medicine.** Proficiency Testing Australia says its reports are under copyright and need its written approval before going to third parties [pta].
Who is already there

items: **RCPAQAP** already applies a language model to participants' answers, under an enterprise arrangement that it says keeps the data out of AI training [rcpaqap-poster].
**The College of American Pathologists** opened a space in 2025 where members try vendors' pathology AI on slide images [cap-studio].

**Collaborative Testing Services**, an American operator of forensic schemes, publishes forensic summary reports on the open web, with each participant's answers under an anonymous code. In one DNA test with 35 participants, a mixture from several people split them: 11 included the suspect, 13 excluded him and 11 called it inconclusive [cts-dna]. A firearms test with 280 respondents produced about 20% false identifications on some items, and the examiners' association investigated [afte].

blocks.text: No company was found licensing an operator's interpretive rounds as an AI test. The idea is not new to the operators, who are building next to it themselves.
What would have to be stripped

Most items hold no patient data, since samples are pooled or anonymised. The Australian operator's privacy policy mentions donor details kept with some tissue [rcpaqap-privacy]. Participant labs are already coded, but in a small round an instrument or method field could point to one lab. Tissue images were given for quality assurance and education; the UK scheme relies on that purpose [ukneqas], and commercial AI use is a different one. An item used to test a model could not safely be reused in a live round.
What stands in the way

items: Nobody has been shown to buy this kind of test, and pathology images and exam-style questions are available elsewhere.
The Australian operator's own terms single out financial gain to others as a reason to refuse.
The American operator is building AI evaluation itself, which sets the pattern that operators and not outsiders run it.

title: Laboratory proficiency tests scored against the known answer

blocks.text: The record
Three records share one form: a person performs a set task against the clock, and an assessor fills in a marking sheet. They do not share a verdict.

**Clinical skills stations.** A medical candidate has a few minutes with an actor in the role of a patient, and an examiner ticks off a checklist as they go. The record is the recording, the station brief and the examiner's sheet.
**Trade practical tests.** An apprentice wires up a board or makes a weld, and an assessor from a training organisation ticks a checklist tied to a national standard.

**Trade-skill competitions.** At WorldSkills events a competitor builds a set project over many hours. Experts mark it part by part. Some parts are marked by measurement, where a gauge reading earns the mark or does not. Others are marked by judgement, where several experts score.

A worked example from the Australian Medical Council, which examines doctors trained overseas. Sitting the clinical exam costs A$3,000 at the test centre or A$3,400 for the online version [amc-exam]. A candidate moves through 16 assessed stations and four rest stations, each of 10 minutes; 14 count towards the result [amc-exam]. At a station the candidate reads the case for 2 minutes, then spends 8 with the actor [amc-exam]. A pass needs 9 of the 14 [amc-exam]. Of the 1,978 candidates in 2018–19, 537 passed, a rate of 27.1% [amc-annual].
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for expert judgement recorded against a rubric, for spoken exchanges with a purpose, and for first-person video of skilled trades. A marked practical exam joins a performance to a grade.
Vendors advertise hourly pay for ungraded video of trade work. For practical exams marked against a rubric, of any kind, no buyer was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**The official clinical exam.** The Australian Medical Council runs its exam at its own test centre, which its 2014 annual report says was fitted with recording equipment [amc-2014]. The Council owns the material and warns of discipline for breaching the security of exam content [amc-exam]. Medical schools hold their own students' archives.

**Paid practice exams.** Small Australian tutors, often run by doctors who passed, sell mock exams. AMC Clinical Guide lists a mock exam at A$150 and says it can be recorded [amc-guide]. OSCE Revisions already sells AI patients and AI grading across more than 1,800 stations, by its own account [osce-revisions]. A tutor's recordings are its own, subject to what each candidate agreed to.

**Trade tests.** Training organisations hold the evidence, which is mostly paper checklists, photographs and supervisors' reports. A Western Australian government fact sheet mentions video only as a fallback way to confirm a supervisor's report [wa-factsheet].

**Competitions.** WorldSkills Australia says each two-year cycle has over 700 regional competitions in 34 regions and more than 6,000 entrants [wsa]. The international body's competition rules of January 2026 say finished projects belong to the organiser and to WorldSkills International together, and may not be used without both parties' permission (rule 10.15); filming at a workstation needs the approval of the manager for that skill (rule 13.3) [ws-rules]. Whether WorldSkills Australia has rules of its own on filming was not established.
Who is already there

items: **A Texas medical school** put AI grading into routine clinical exams in 2025, published the work in October 2026, and its university has filed patent applications [maples].

**A 2026 preprint** compared an AI grader with examiners on 240 transcripts and 8,405 checklist items [cn-osce]. Where the two disagreed, blinded experts' majority view matched the AI 65.5% of the time and the examiner 27.9% [cn-osce]. Examiners had been lenient.
**Tradeye** gives away narrated first-person video of plumbing, electrical and heating work, more than 1,020 clips by its count [tradeye-hf]. It is ungraded.
**East China Normal University** showed, at a WorldSkills conference in 2026, a system that films students' work from their own viewpoint and grades it against expert rubrics [ws-conf].

blocks.text: Clinical recordings and ungraded trade video are both well supplied. Nobody outside China was found selling measured competition work filmed from the competitor's viewpoint.
What would have to be stripped

Every clinical recording shows the candidate, the actor and the examiner by face and voice, so each person's consent matters. One tutor advertises teaching from recent real exam cases [firstaid-amc], and anything built on recalled cases would meet the Council's claim over its content. School students can enter regional trade competitions [wsa], so some competitors are minors.
What stands in the way

items: Nothing shows that a lab pays more when footage carries a grade than when it does not.
For clinical exams, the examiner's sheet is a weak label, schools supply themselves, and AI tutors already exist.
Competition footage needs two owners' permission, and a Chinese university has already shown its system at the organiser's own conference.

title: Practical exams marked against a fixed sheet

blocks.text: The record
Two records sit on this page. Both come out weak, for different reasons.

**Simulator sessions.** A trainee flies an aircraft, steers a ship or works a mining machine in a simulator. Several times each second the simulator stores what the trainee did with the controls and how the vehicle responded. An instructor marks the session. The record is the inputs, the motion and the mark.

**Harbour pilots' recordings.** A marine pilot comes aboard to bring a ship to its berth, carrying a portable unit: a tablet fed by an accurate satellite receiver of its own and by the ship's identification transmitter. The screen gives the ship's position and heading, how fast it is turning and how fast each end is approaching the berth. The passage is stored for replay.

An illustration, not a real file, with one real figure. A bulk carrier takes on a pilot at the entrance to Port Phillip, where about 5,800 large commercial ships are piloted in a year [ga-pilots]. The unit begins recording when it is switched on, and for about two hours logs where the ship is and how it is turning. The result is the speed at the moment of touching and whether anything was struck.

What the pilot's recording leaves out decides the matter. When a ship struck a bridge in Baltimore, the US transport safety board's laboratory examined the log from the pilot's unit. It found the ship's identification messages and separate readings for heading and rate of turn [ntsb]. Orders to the helm, the engine and the tugs were absent, and so was voice. Those are on the ship's own black box. The pilot's unit records where the ship went, not what the pilot did.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for records of experts controlling machines with every action attached, such as game play with controller inputs and remote operation of robots. A graded simulator log has that form. A pilot's track without actions does not.
No lab or vendor was found asking for ship, aircraft or mining-machine operation, and no buyer was found for either record.
Who holds it and who may share it

**Airline simulators.** CAE, a Canadian training company, sells a system that collects data from its simulators alongside instructors' electronic grades [cae]. The airlines own their crews' training records. A template agreement from the international pilots' federation says outside parties may seek flight data for safety purposes, that anonymised data can go to them if the pilots' association is told on each occasion, and that data which is only useful when tied to particular flights needs the association's agreement [ifalpa]. Sale to an AI company is not addressed in the template.

**Ship simulators.** The Australian Maritime College in Launceston has a full bridge simulator and tug simulators and trains pilots for several ports and resource companies [amc-sim]. The centre holds the logs. Who owns them depends on each training contract, and none was seen.
**Mining simulators.** Immersive Technologies of Perth says it works with more than 360 sites, and that it monitors how operators brake, change gear and manage speed [immersive].

**Pilots' recordings.** The firms and port corporations that provide pilots hold them. The Australasian pilots' institute's code of practice says recording should begin automatically, that recordings should be kept safe and archived, and that the policy belongs in the provider's safety system [ampi]. No statute on who owns the recordings was found.
**The ship's black box.** A circular of the International Maritime Organization, issued in 2002, says the shipowner owns the recorder and its information in all circumstances [imo].
Who is already there

items: **CAE** and **Immersive Technologies** each use their own sector's simulator data themselves.

**OMC International** sells analysis of pilotage performance to ports and has published a position on the ethical use of such data, covering what pilots should be told about collection, access, retention and discipline [omc].
**Researchers** at a Japanese university built a berthing planner by imitation learning based on ship-tracking (AIS) data, and verified it with data from one port [osaka].

blocks.text: No seller of pilots' tracks to AI companies turned up, and public tracking data supports the same research at lower precision.
What would have to be stripped

A named pilot's or trainee's performance is personal information and belongs to their employment history. The pilots' bodies whose documents were read want such data used for learning and not for punishment. Simulator models are licensed from manufacturers, as Immersive says of its own [immersive], and such licences may limit use of the logs.
What stands in the way

items: No buyer: no lab or vendor is on record asking for this kind of operation.
The pilot's unit records no actions. The actions are on the black box, which belongs to the shipowner.
Each simulator sector has an incumbent using the data, under manufacturers' licences on the models.
Pilots' bodies' stance on performance data.
