blocks.text: The record

A veterinary clinic keeps a file on each animal. It records the reason for the visit, the vet's findings, which tests were ordered and what they showed, the diagnosis, the treatment, the charge, and what had happened by the next visit. The file lives in the clinic's practice software, the system that handles bookings, records and billing.

An illustration, not a real file: a cat of about ten is brought in because it is losing weight and drinking heavily. The vet writes up the history and the examination. Blood and urine go to a laboratory and the results return into the file. The diagnosis is early kidney disease. A special diet is prescribed, with a recheck in three months. At the recheck the weight and blood values are entered again. Some years later the file closes with the animal's death. That is one case followed from complaint to outcome, every step dated, and none of it subject to the laws that guard human medical records.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for real records of professional work with the outcome attached, and for healthcare material. A veterinary file is clinical reasoning with a result, without a human patient.
No lab was found asking for veterinary records. Sellers exist and quote prices. No purchase by a named AI lab was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**The clinic owns the file.** The veterinary board of Victoria says in its guideline on records that a medical record is the property of the practice or practitioner who made it and not of the animal's owner, and that the vet keeps the owner's personal information confidential [vic-board]. The same board expects records to move with a practice when it is sold [vic-board]. In New South Wales the code of conduct in the Veterinary Practice Regulation 2013 says a practitioner must keep confidential what is learned in practice, and that records are kept for at least 3 years [nsw-reg]; the copy read is the regulation as it stood in 2017. Other states' rules were not opened.

**Who holds files in Australia.** VetPartners says it has more than 270 clinics and hospitals across Australia and New Zealand [vetpartners]. A university group, VetCompass Australia, holds over 15 million records from 180 clinics for research, which a paper puts at 5% of the country's clinics [vet-paper].

**The software company in the middle.** IDEXX owns ezyVet, a practice system. Its terms say the clinic owns its data, and also that the clinic permits the company to use it to improve the software, to pool it, and to pass it to third parties with the clinic and its customers made unidentifiable [ezyvet-terms]. IDEXX's master terms give it a perpetual, royalty-free licence over diagnostic images that clinics submit [idexx-master]. Other software companies' terms were not opened.
Who is already there

items: **Sikka** connects to practice software and sells to AI developers now. It offers two things: anonymised records on a yearly licence, and hosted practice environments in which an AI agent works a clinic's system and is scored on what really happened, priced from $252,000 a year [sikka]. It says its coverage is the United States and Canada and that it is expanding into Australia [sikka].
**Evident** pulls diagnoses, treatments and outcomes out of clinics' free-text notes and sells them to drug, research and pet-food companies, sharing revenue with the clinics [evident].
**Sage Veterinary Imaging** licenses scans with specialists' reports to AI labs, including trial batches of 500 to 1,000 studies [sage].
**A British university project** gives away 17,600 annotated records under an open licence [peteval].
University groups have trained models on these archives; one American group says it is unable to share the 246,473 visits it coded by hand [vet-paper].

blocks.text: The record is not untouched. One seller with thousands of practices already prices both the raw records and the practice environment, and has named Australia as its next market.
What would have to be stripped

The owner's name, address, phone, email and payment details; the clinic's and staff members' names. Free-text notes carry all of these, and sometimes the owner's own health or family circumstances. The duties of confidence above bind each vet personally, so a careless sale could put the seller's right to practise at risk.
What stands in the way

items: No lab has been shown to want veterinary data.
A seller far larger than any Australian holder is already in the market and is entering Australia.
The main software company's terms let it pass on anonymised clinic data itself.
Cleaning free-text notes is costly, and each vet carries a duty of confidence.

title: Veterinary records, from first complaint to outcome

blocks.text: The record
Large insurers do not license their claim files. This page looks at the same kind of file in three places where someone else owns it. The three get different verdicts.

**The policyholder's claims professional.** A loss assessor, called a public adjuster in the United States, works for the person claiming and not for the insurer, usually for a share of whatever is recovered. The file holds the policy, photographs, the assessor's estimate, the insurer's first offer or refusal, the correspondence and the final settlement.

**Companies that insure themselves.** A company may carry its own risk under a licence to self-insure injuries at work, or through an insurance company it owns. It keeps its own files, from the injury report and medical certificates to the final settlement.

**Sold-off old claims.** An insurer that leaves a line of business can pass its unsettled claims to a specialist buyer, which pays them out, sometimes over decades. The file is years of claim notes, legal advice, medical reports, the reserve held from time to time and the last payment.

An illustration, not a real file, with invented round figures. Hail damages a house. The insurer's inspector offers $36,000. The owner hires a public adjuster for a fee of a tenth of the payout. The adjuster reads the policy, finds a clause covering the cost of meeting current building rules, writes an itemised estimate and asks for more. The insurer adds $12,000. The final payment is $48,000 and the fee is $4,800. The file holds two rival estimates of one loss, the argument, and the figure both sides accepted.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for finance and insurance records, for expert judgement with its reasoning, and for checks that are hard to game. A policyholder-side file offers both sides' numbers and a result the other side agreed to.

No lab has been shown buying records labelled with their outcome, here or elsewhere. The evidence is indirect: Huzzle Labs is building a test from real policies and claim files, scored against the recorded outcome, with sensitive material removed or replaced [huzzle].
Who holds it and who may share it

**Loss assessors.** In Australia, a guidance sheet from the corporate regulator says that since January 2022 a person paid to pursue a claim on a policyholder's behalf needs a financial services licence that covers claims handling [asic-253]. Several firms are tied to repair builders, so many files end in a repair and not in a negotiated sum. The working file is the firm's, and the policyholder is the firm's client.

**Self-insurers.** Regulators publish the lists: New South Wales names banks, supermarkets, a university and local councils [sira], and Victoria lists 33 [worksafe-vic]. A self-insurer stands as the insurer and the files are its own.
**Buyers of old claims.** A trade magazine counted 42 public deals in 2025, moving about US$5.4 billion of reserves [runoff-mag]. After a full legal transfer the buyer owns the files.

**Privacy.** The Australian privacy regulator's guidance on the principle governing use and disclosure says personal information may be used only for the purpose it was collected for, and that for sensitive information, which includes health information, a second purpose needs consent or a direct relation to the first [oaic-app6]. The guidance does not mention AI training.
Who is already there

items: **InsureThing** released a test of 160 tasks in 2026, written by specialists and not drawn from closed files [insurething].
**A Chinese university group** published 3,780 cases built on real claim materials and expanded by a language model; the best model scored 73.15% on decision and amount together [insclaimbench].
**Tailshift** is itself a buyer of old liability claims, and says it holds broad sets of claim notes and legal and medical records, which it uses to price deals [tailshift].

blocks.text: No one turned up licensing files from the policyholder's side that show the first offer and the final payment. The test built from claim files, however, already has several entrants.
What would have to be stripped

Property files hold names, addresses, pictures of homes and policy numbers: ordinary personal data. Injury files hold named people's medical histories, which are hard to anonymise when a rare injury happens at a known employer. Old-claims files add legal advice and confidentiality terms owed to the original insurer.
What stands in the way

items: No buyer has been shown for claims labelled with their outcome, while several tests already cover the ground.
The final payment is a bargain struck between two sides, not a correct answer.
For injury files, consent and anonymising are costly.
Buyers of old claims treat the data as their advantage and will not sell it.
In Australia there are few such files, and a good share finish with a builder's repair.

title: Insurance claim files held outside the big insurers

blocks.text: The record

Australia sets minimum pay through legal instruments called modern awards, one for each industry or occupation. An award lays down job levels, ordinary hours, higher rates for nights, weekends and public holidays, overtime, and allowances. Award interpretation is the name for working out the correct pay for a given person on a given shift.

An employer that discovers past mistakes carries out a remediation, going back over old shifts for the staff affected and paying what is missing. The record is a pair: the amount payroll paid for a shift, and the amount the recalculation finds was due, with the reason they differ.

An illustration, not a real file: a casual shop worker is rostered on a Sunday from early afternoon into the late evening, with one unpaid break. Payroll paid eight hours at the ordinary casual rate. The recalculation applies the Sunday rate, a late-evening rule, and a penalty because the break came too late in the shift. The gap for that shift is about $40. The same working is then repeated for several hundred shifts and several thousand employees.

The totals are real. The workplace regulator, the Fair Work Ombudsman, says that in 2024–25 it got back A$358 million on behalf of more than 249,000 workers [fwo-2025]. Its register of binding undertakings by employers lists the University of Melbourne at A$72 million for more than 25,000 staff [fwo-register].
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for practice tasks with checks that cannot be gamed, and for accounting work. A pay answer is right or wrong to the cent. Australian payroll advisers have written publicly that chatbots get penalty rates wrong with confidence [valont].
No lab or vendor was found buying pay-calculation data or tasks. The work is specific to one country; to a foreign lab it would stand in for applying a long rulebook exactly to untidy facts.
Who holds it and who may share it
Both the payroll data and the recalculation belong to the employer. Three other groups hold copies or tools.

items: **Remediation software firms.** PaidRight, of Melbourne, describes the job as gathering payroll data, applying a model of the award, and analysing the gap between paid and owed, with 80 to 120 data points in each calculation [paidright].
**Accounting firms, law firms and payroll software companies** hold working papers and encoded rules.

blocks.text: Two things limit what an employer may pass on.

Privacy. The Australian privacy regulator's guidance says the exemption for employee records reaches only what an employer itself does in direct connection with the employment, and does not cover contractors handling the records of another organisation's staff [oaic-exemption]. Whether handing pay records to a data buyer falls outside the exemption was not tested in anything opened.

Legal privilege. A law firm's published guidance says employers commonly have lawyers lead the work so that the analysis is privileged, and that existing payroll records do not become privileged merely by being handed to a lawyer [pointon]. On that account the raw timesheets are not protected and the corrected model often is. No court decision on that exact point was found.

**The public side is unusually full.** The Fair Work Commission publishes a database of over 70,000 award pay rates, allowances and penalty rates, free to download and query [fwc-db]. The awards themselves are public. The regulator runs a free official pay calculator [fwo-calc].
Who is already there

items: **PaidRight** and **Yellow Canary** sell remediation and ongoing checking, built on their own encoded award logic.

blocks.text: No public test that takes an award and a roster and asks for the correct pay was found. Nor was any sale of remediation data.

What matters more is that the private records are unnecessary. A remediation is checked by software that encodes the rules, guided by a lawyer's view of what the award means. It is not a verdict from an opposing party. A competent payroll specialist with the published awards and rates can write pay tasks with exact answers.
What would have to be stripped

Names, staff numbers, tax and bank details, dates of birth, and the names of small sites. Remediation reports raise privilege, and an employer that has given a public undertaking has little wish to see its pattern of errors circulate.
What stands in the way

items: No private data is needed, so nothing keeps others out. The public version can be built by anyone.
No buyer has been identified, and the task is specific to Australia.
The right answer is open to dispute at the edges, such as which award covers a job. Courts decide those, and they are the cases without a clean check.
A model may reach exact pay by calling a rules engine as a tool, which leaves little for training to add.

blocks.text: The record

In Australia, personal financial advice to an ordinary client must be given under a licence. The licence holder, called the licensee, carries the legal responsibility and must be able to show the advice served the client's interests. What proves it is the advice file. It contains the client's circumstances and goals, a measure of their appetite for risk, notes, product research, and a long document, the Statement of Advice, giving the recommendation and the reasons. A technician called a paraplanner usually builds that document from the adviser's brief.
Two kinds of verdict are attached to these files, and they come out differently.

**The check before release.** Before the document goes to the client, a compliance reviewer at the licensee tests it against a list of questions, then either clears it or returns it with a list of faults.
**The review after misconduct.** When wrongdoing is found, every affected file is reviewed again. The reviewer decides whether the advice was suitable and, if it was not, works out compensation.

An illustration, not a real file: a couple in their late fifties want to retire in five years. A paraplanner models moving both their retirement accounts to a new provider and drafts a sixty-page document. The reviewer fails it, because nothing compares the fees and insurance of the old accounts with the new. The comparison, once added, shows the couple would lose a large amount of life cover. The recommendation changes to keep one account, and the file passes.

The second verdict has real numbers. The corporate regulator's final count, to the end of 2022, shows six institutions paid or offered A$4.7 billion [asic-final]. Of that, A$4,416,195,480 went to 1,590,689 customers who were charged fees for no service, which is a billing check [asic-final]. The part that turned on a judgement about advice was far smaller: 11,968 customers shared A$270,208,386 [asic-final]. Westpac had 3,341 of them, NAB 3,034, AMP 2,844, ANZ 2,123 and CBA 626 [asic-final].
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for finance work, for expert judgement with its reasoning, and for real work across several tools. A draft, the findings against it and the corrected draft make a trace of a decision.
Nothing found shows a purchase of advice-compliance files, Australian or otherwise. A reviewer's pass is also an opinion and not an outcome.
Who holds it and who may share it
Adviser Ratings counted 15,084 advisers at the start of 2026 [adviser-ratings]. No national count of advice documents was found.

**The licensee** is the file's owner and has to keep it. A regulator's instrument of 2024 sets the period at 7 years from the day of the advice, and that the duty continues even if the licensee stops being licensed [asic-records].

**Compliance software companies** hold the pairs of interest. Advice RegTech describes its product as a system of record for pre-release checks and audits [adviceregtech]. iComply2 sells AI review of advice documents and whole-file audits [icomply2].

**Review records.** The regulator's guide on remediation says licensees should document their approach, decisions, progress and outcomes for consumers, and that the regulator may ask to see those records [rg277]. The files mostly concern advice given years ago and are nearing the end of the retention period.
Who is already there

items: **Advice RegTech** took part in the regulator's 2019 trial, in which its software read advice documents and flagged fee errors, missing alternatives and mismatched risk profiles [asic-trial].

**The market's stated norm.** A guide for advisers published in October 2026 tells practices to question each vendor about training on client data and to choose tools whose terms rule it out [whatcould].

blocks.text: No dataset, test or paper drawing on Australian advice files turned up, and no seller of files. Nobody licenses them, which here means they are locked and not that they were overlooked.
What would have to be stripped

An advice file is a financial life story: names, birth dates, tax numbers, income, assets, debts, health disclosures made for insurance, and family and inheritance details. Blanking names is not enough in a long narrative about one household, where age, job, employer's fund, suburb and balances together point to the people. The privacy rules on reusing such information were not opened for this dossier.
What stands in the way

items: The files are dense personal histories, costly to anonymise, in a market that expects them never to be used for training.
No buyer has been shown, and the rules are Australian.
The verdict attached is a compliance opinion, not an outcome.
The reviewed files are ageing out of the retention period and sit with banks that have no reason to release them.
The software companies that hold the checks could build on them without anyone's help.

blocks.text: The record
Three records sit on this page, and each has its own verdict.

**The whole declaration with its later correction.** Every commercial shipment entering a country is declared to the border agency. A declaration names the goods and gives the tariff code that sets the duty, the value, where they were made and whether a trade agreement lowers the duty. A licensed customs broker usually files it for the importer. Some declarations are checked later, by a request for documents, an audit, a penalty or a refund. A checked declaration is professional work with an outside verdict: the original line, the documents behind it, the finding and the corrected line.
**The tariff code alone.** Choosing the code for a product, taken as a task by itself.

**Freight invoice disputes.** A shipper agrees rates with carriers. Each carrier's invoice is checked against the contract, mismatches are disputed, and the carrier gives a credit or refuses with proof. The record is the invoice, the contract terms, the dispute and the carrier's reply.

A worked example from the Australian border agency's own monitoring. Over nine months of the 2024–25 year it checked 5,226 import declaration lines [abf-update]. It found errors in 1,579 of them, which is 30.2% [abf-update]. The most common error was the tariff code, with 351 detections [abf-update]. So roughly three checked lines in ten were wrong somewhere, and the code was the commonest fault.

An illustration of one corrected file, not a real one: a broker files insulated steel bottles as general household steelware and claims a trade-agreement discount. An audit later finds the wrong code, a discount certificate that did not cover the supplier, and a wrong value.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for long office work on real documents and for checks that are hard to game. Here the check comes from a party with the opposite interest: the agency collecting the duty, or the carrier that sent the bill. That is rarer than an expert's opinion.
No purchase of whole declarations with corrections, or of freight disputes, by a lab or a vendor was found.
Who holds it and who may share it
The importer owns its declarations. The broker holds copies as the importer's agent. The broker's software company processes them. The agency holds the outcomes.

**United States.** The customs agency ruled in January 2026 on who may share them. Its ruling restates the regulation that keeps a broker's client records confidential unless a court orders disclosure or the client authorises it in writing, then says the regulation "does not constrain an importer's ability to divulge its own records" [cbp-ruling]. The same ruling says a company without a broker's licence is doing customs business impermissibly if its AI tool suggests codes beyond the six-digit level for goods that will be entered [cbp-ruling]. The ruling thus separates sharing past records from advising on live shipments.

**Australia.** The border agency's guide to penalty notices says owners must keep commercial documents for 5 years [abf-guide]. No rule matching the American confidentiality regulation was found in the broker licence conditions that were read. That is a gap in this dossier and not a finding.
**Freight.** The shipper owns its invoices and disputes; the audit firm processes them. Cass Information Systems says that in 2025 it handled 35 million freight invoices, worth US$37 billion [cass].
Who is already there

The tariff code alone is well covered in public. A research group released 18,731 published American rulings, covering 2,992 codes, as a training and test set; the general model it tested scored 25% on the full ten-digit code and a fine-tuned open model 40% [atlas]. A second test used 632 online shop products labelled by 26 tariff experts; the best AI agent scored 46.8% against 95.0% for the experts [hscodecomp].

Several companies train on their own flow. Zonos says its classifier learns from official rulings and from the product listings it sees daily [zonos]. WiseTech, a maker of freight-forwarding software, publishes terms for its AI agents saying the customer always owns its data and that none is extracted [wisetech]. In freight, Loop says its software audits invoices against contracts and opens and tracks disputes with carriers [loop].

What no public set holds is the whole declaration with a real correction, covering code, value, origin and discount together with the documents. Freight disputes with carriers' replies sit only with the firms that process them.
What would have to be stripped

There is little personal information: named contacts, sole traders, brokers' staff. The sensitive content is commercial. Who the suppliers are, what each unit costs and how much is bought are trade secrets, and an audit finding records the importer's own mistake, so only files already settled with the agency would be suitable.
What stands in the way

items: Nobody has been shown to want it. Demand for logistics records is voiced by middlemen, not buyers.
The best-known part of the task is already public, which holds down the value of anything nearby.
Most declarations are never checked. Those that end in a real correction are few and arrive years late.
Importers are reluctant to hand over supplier prices and evidence of their own errors.
The software companies that process declarations and freight bills can build on them without anyone's help.

When a company stops trading it leaves behind its whole working history: email, chat, shared drives, the accounting ledger, the customer database, job and ticket systems, contracts and code. If the company is insolvent, the files go to a liquidator or an administrator: an accountant, registered for the purpose, who sells whatever remains and pays the creditors. If the company is solvent and is being closed on purpose, which is called a members' voluntary liquidation, its directors and shareholders remain on hand and can sign.

The numbers, as reported from the corporate regulator's statistics: in the 2025–26 financial year 14,152 companies went into external administration for the first time [accountants-daily]. Most are small. Of the administrators' reports lodged in 2022–23, 82% concerned companies with fewer than 20 employees, and 83% concerned companies with assets of A$100,000 or less [asic-23-346mr].

No Australian sale of such records was found. The model case is American. A transcription company called cielo24 closed after more than a decade [simpleclosure-blog]. Its shutdown agent, SimpleClosure, says it found a language-technology buyer for the company's data assets, which paid what it calls "mid-six figures" [simpleclosure-blog].
Why it might matter for training AI
Data vendors' own pages show labs asking for the internal records of ordinary companies.

The trade exists in the United States at small size. SimpleClosure says more than 350 companies have listed with it, and forecasts that it will return more than US$10 million to them by the end of 2026 [simpleclosure-pr]. The one large price on record is a bid, not a sale: Google offered US$10 million for the records of the failed Spirit Airlines [spirit-auction-notice], and the court has not approved it. No purchase of Australian company records by a lab or a vendor was found.
Who holds it and who may share it
The company owns its records. The liquidator's or administrator's firm holds them. Microsoft, Google, Xero and Slack only host them, and the accounts lapse when the bills stop.

The Corporations Act, section 477(2)(c), says a liquidator may "sell or otherwise dispose of, in any manner, all or any part of the property of the company" [corps-act-477]. Whether a mailbox or a shared drive counts as property under that section was not established. The regulator's guidance says whoever was the final external administrator has to hold on to the company's books for five years once the administration is over [asic-rg81], so the records usually survive long after anyone has reason to open them.

Privacy law is the harder part. The Privacy Act normally leaves small businesses alone, but section 6D removes that exemption from anyone who "discloses personal information about another individual to anyone else for a benefit, service or advantage", unless the person consented or a law authorises it [privacy-act-6d]. A law firm's note for liquidators, published in 2024, says a distressed company is "unlikely to hold the exceedingly broad consents that would be required", and that "it is unlikely the court would approve an order allowing for the explicit sale of personal information" [hwle-2024]. The court decision that note relies on was not itself read.

One Australian precedent points the other way, on narrower facts. When the retailer Dick Smith failed in 2016, its receivers told customers before the customer database went to another retailer and let them opt out [dick-smith-asx]. That was a customer list passing to a similar shop, not staff email passing to an AI lab.
Who is already there

items: SimpleClosure, in the United States, sells source code and "workspace data" for closing startups and does its own stripping of personal data [simpleclosure-assethub].
The General Data Company, with a San Francisco address, offers the "document estates of wound-down European companies" under what it calls a "written administrator mandate" [general-data-insolvency].
Tonic.ai sells the stripping of personal data as a service for this trade, and argues that whoever does it should be independent of the broker [tonic-usecase].
An Irish law firm told insolvency practitioners in September 2026 that operational data "may warrant consideration" as an asset [william-fry].

blocks.text: The buyers look to America first. micro1's page asks for companies with "30+ employees" and says "We currently prioritize US companies, followed by other Western markets" [micro1-data-partnerships].
No Australian operator, professional guidance or law-firm note on sales for AI training was found.
What would have to be stripped

Everything that identifies a person: staff, customers, suppliers' contacts. The 2024 note says "Any appropriately aggregated or de-identified information is outside the scope" of the privacy principles entirely [hwle-2024]. Whether the stripping step is itself a permitted use of the records was not established. Supplier and customer contracts carry their own confidentiality terms, and legal advice held in the files is privileged.
What stands in the way

items: No buyer has been shown to want Australian company records.
Most failed companies are below the size buyers ask for.
The published legal view is sceptical that personal information can be sold out of a liquidation, and a liquidator is personally exposed for a small sum.

The Spirit Airlines hearing was moved to 6 November 2026, according to one press report [travel-weekly]. More than 120 members of Congress have asked that employee records be left out [technology-org]. Insolvency lawyers everywhere will read the outcome.

blocks.text: The record
Two public stocks of real internal documents, each with an official conclusion attached.

The first is inquiry exhibits. A royal commission is a public inquiry with the power to compel documents. The documents it relied on are published as exhibits: emails, papers that went to boards, briefing notes and notes for file. A report with findings follows. Australia's inquiries into banking, the Robodebt welfare scheme, aged care and two casino operators each published exhibits this way.

The second is planning examination libraries. In England and Wales a very large project, such as a major road, wind farm or power station, is examined in public by an appointed panel. All of it is filed in a numbered library, from the application through the panel's rounds of written questions and the replies to them, down to the panel's recommendation and the decision the minister takes.

A worked example from one real library, for the Keadby Next Generation Power Station [keadby-library]. The application documents are numbered from APP-001 [keadby-library]. The panel's first written questions are document PD-008 [keadby-library]. The applicant and the objectors answer at the first deadline. The draft consent order, the legal instrument that would permit the project, is then revised at successive deadlines, from revision 3 through to a final revision 6 dated 16 June 2026 [keadby-library]. A test question could give an AI system the application together with that first round of questions, then ask which conditions the panel will insist on changing, and mark the answer against the tracked changes and the recommendation.
Why it might matter for training AI

Data vendors' pages show labs asking for long office work on real documents and for tests that are hard to game. Both stocks offer real documents with an official outcome to mark against. What could be sold is a private set of test questions with marking guides, not the documents.
No purchase by a lab of a test built from inquiry or planning documents was found.
Who holds it and who may share it
The host of the documents is not their owner. Each document belongs to whoever wrote it.

The Robodebt commission's site says its material is under a Creative Commons Attribution licence "with the exception of ... content supplied by third parties", and that where a third party holds copyright, "Their permission may be required to use the material" [robodebt-copyright]. Whether the exhibits fall inside or outside that licence is not stated there and was not established. In the banking inquiry the exhibits were written inside the banks; its copyright page could not be opened.

The Planning Inspectorate's terms say: "We do not authorise the use or republishing of third party documents without the permission of the original intellectual property holder" [pins-terms]. That covers everything written by applicants and objectors. The panel's own questions and reports are the government's.

So no single party is able to license either stock in full. The official side, which is the side that does the marking, can be reused with attribution. The exhibits and applications cannot be passed on without each author's permission.

On copyright more broadly, Australia's Attorney-General said in October 2025 that the government was "ruling out a Text and Data Mining Exception" [ag-2025]. How Australian or American copyright law would treat a commercial test set built from these documents was not established; the relevant statutes and cases were not opened.
Who is already there
Nothing built on royal commission exhibits turned up: no dataset, no test, no product. The same goes for the planning libraries.

The Planning Inspectorate's guidance now asks parties to say when they have used AI to prepare a submission [pins-advice], which suggests consultants already use AI systems on these documents in private.
What would have to be stripped

People are named in the exhibits, among them junior officials, bank employees and bank customers. The Robodebt and aged-care exhibits include vulnerable people. Objectors' names and addresses appear in planning submissions. Test questions would have to avoid turning on a named individual's conduct.

One design avoids most of the copyright problem: supply a pointer to each public document and a freshly written question, with the marking guide drawn from the official report, and let the buyer fetch the document itself.
What stands in the way

items: Nobody has been shown to buy a ready-made test of this kind from an unknown seller.

The famous outcomes are public. An AI system may recall what a commissioner found without reasoning from the documents. Whether public web crawls hold these documents was not established here; a single crawl would prove little, since labs gather the web themselves.

Only decisions made after an AI system was trained are clean. Planning decisions keep arriving: for one offshore wind project the recommendation was dated 14 May 2026 and the order was made on 8 June 2026 [dogger-bank-south].
A pointer file with marking guides is something a lab could rebuild itself.
Commission findings are judgements about conduct, which are harder to mark without argument than a planning panel's document-by-document changes.
A commercial product built on the files of people harmed by a government scheme would be badly received.

Each line of this log carries three numbers, and now and then a typed note. The first number is the software's proposal, the second is the figure a person put in its place, and the third is the outcome. It turns up in three trades.

In demand planning, a program predicts how much of every product will sell in the coming month. A planner raises or lowers some of the forecasts, often typing a reason. Actual sales arrive weeks later.
In retail buying, quantities are ordered months in advance and prices are cut as the season goes on. The result is how much of the stock sold at each price.
In hotels, a pricing system suggests what to charge for a room on every coming night. The hotel's revenue manager takes the suggestion or changes it. Bookings follow.

An illustration, not a real file: the system forecasts sales of 10,000 cases of a drink for December. The planner raises it to 13,000 and types "retailer promotion, week 50". Actual sales are 10,000. The system was right and the planner was 3,000 cases too high. The trade calls this comparison "forecast value added": did the human step make the forecast better than the step before it?
Why it might matter for training AI
The appeal is an expert decision with a hard check. Sales figures do not flatter anyone.
No lab or vendor was found buying records of this kind. Those found using them are consultancies and the makers of planning software, each working on one customer's data at a time.
Who holds it and who may share it
The company whose planners made the changes owns the record. The software company processes it. What the published contracts say differs by vendor.

IDeaS, which sells hotel pricing software, says in its acceptable use policy that its reporting and extraction tools "must not be used to provide data to third parties without explicit approval from IDeaS" [ideas-aup]. Read plainly, a hotel could not send its history to a data buyer without that approval.

PROS, a pricing-software company, says in its subscription agreement that "Customer retains all right, title and interest in and to all Customer Data", and that it will use de-identified customer data for its own machine learning [pros-msa].

For several other large planning vendors no published customer terms were found. One point was not established anywhere: whether the stored system forecast, which is the vendor's output, counts as the customer's data.
Who is already there
The bare record is already public and well studied.

A 2025 paper in the International Journal of Forecasting pooled "the publicly available data on around 147,000 forecasts from six studies" [ijf-2025]. It found that human adjustments improved the forecasts "for only just over half" of products, and that evidence of forecasters making good use of information the software lacked was weak [ijf-2025].

Two consultancies have trained on one client's log each. First Analytics says that on a test of 900,000 overrides its machine and the planners were "virtually tied" [first-analytics]. EyeOn says the direction and size of a change predicted whether it helped, and that the written explanations "had only a limited impact on the model’s predictions" [eyeon].

For hotels, an economics paper studied about 6 million price observations from 9 hotels, holding the system's recommendation, the manager's price and the bookings [cesifo-10849]. It reports that about 85% of managers' price updates copy the recommendation exactly [cesifo-10849].
The software companies learn from customers' overrides inside their own products, as the PROS and SAP terms allow.
What does not exist in public is a large set from many companies with the surrounding context. Nobody has been shown to want one.
What would have to be stripped
Little of it is personal: planners' user names and names typed into comment fields. Hotel booking records carry guest details, which would be left out.

The sensitive content is commercial. Suppliers' cost prices, promotion plans agreed with particular customers and retailers' trading terms are held alongside the forecasts, and are usually covered by confidentiality clauses with third parties. Pooling forward prices from competing hotels raises competition concerns; the hotel paper's authors chose hotels with no neighbouring client of the same system, which they say reduces "concerns about algorithmic collusion" [cesifo-10849].
What stands in the way

items: Nobody has been found buying planning records that come with outcomes.
The signal is thin. The best pooled study finds the human change helps only about half the time, and one consultancy found the typed reason adds little.
A public pool of the bare record already exists.

By itself the log is a few numbers and a brief note. To be useful it would need what the planner could see when deciding: sales history, the promotion calendar, stock and customer emails. That is most of a company's records, not a log.
Some vendor terms forbid passing the data on, and third parties' trading terms sit inside it.
The software companies already do the learning inside their products and gain nothing by releasing the data.

blocks.text: The record

A competition can be designed so that what it leaves behind is a professional's reasoning, in writing, about a real case, plus an independent fact showing whether that reasoning held up. This page covers two versions, and they come out differently.

**The case contest.** The organiser has a stock of cases that are finished but whose results were never published: insurance claims, disputes, loans. Each entrant studies a file, says how it ended and explains the call. The real outcome scores them. A forward-looking variant uses decisions that have not yet been made.

**The drill-target challenge.** A miner opens up its exploration data and entrants propose drilling spots, with reasons. The best proposals get drilled, and the score is the laboratory's reading of how much metal the rock holds.

A worked example of the drill version, from a real contest. In 2019 OZ Minerals, a miner, ran the Explorer Challenge with Unearthed, a contest platform, offering a prize pool of A$1 million, drawing "over one thousand global participants from sixty-two countries" [unearthed-2019]. The company then drilled "the top consensus targets ... in an initial program of 5 holes for 2,503.1m", and reported that "no significant mineralisation was intersected" [ozl-q4-2019]. Five scored outcomes, all negative.
Why it might matter for training AI
A real case with a real result is hard to fake, and data vendors' pages show labs asking for expert judgement and for tests that cannot be gamed.

What was found shows interest in forecasting as a test of AI systems, not as something bought from people. Metaculus, a forecasting site, runs tournaments for AI bots [metaculus-aib]. Mantic, a company building forecasting systems, says it raised US$25 million [mantic]. No price paid by a lab for human forecasters' written reasoning was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**The reasoning.** What an entrant writes is the entrant's, unless the rules of the contest transfer or license it. Since the organiser drafts those rules, ownership can be settled cleanly from the start. The terms of the two mining contests on this point were not read.
**The cases.** They belong to the insurer, lender, law firm or dispute body that handled them. If the outcomes are public, as court judgments are, an AI system may already have seen them.
**The drilling data and results.** They belong to the mining company.

On Australian contest law, Victoria's gambling regulator advises anyone running a commercial-scale tipping competition online to take legal advice on the federal interactive gambling law [vgccc]. The statutes themselves were not opened, so how an outcome-prediction contest would be classed was not established.
Who is already there
Every component exists.

items: **Mining.** Besides the Explorer Challenge, a Canadian contest in 2016 offered C$1 million for targets on an old gold mine [integra]. No drilling result from it was found.

**Forecasting.** Metaculus runs FutureEval to measure the forecasting accuracy of AI [metaculus-futureeval]. Mantic says its system beat all 676 human entrants in one Metaculus contest in 2026 [mantic].
**Law.** A research paper gave 200 American class-action complaints to legal experts, who predicted the outcome correctly 53% of the time against 63% for a small AI system [classaction-paper].

**Insurance.** A paper from October 2026 describes a test of 3,780 claim cases "grounded in real claim materials" [insclaimbench]. A broker, DataNexx, lists closed insurance claims with "assessor reports ... and settlement outcomes" for licence [datanexx].

blocks.text: What was not found is a contest set up in order to sell labs the scored reasoning of practitioners.
What would have to be stripped

For the case contest, the files carry personal and sensitive information, and every limit that binds the holder of the files passes through to the organiser. An entrant who works in the field must not draw on an employer's knowledge of the actual case. The purpose of the contest, including any use for training AI, would have to be told to entrants at the start.
For the drill version there is nothing personal. The constraint is when a listed company may release its results.
What stands in the way
**The case contest**

items: No buyer for human forecasting reasoning has been shown.
Professionals are not reliably better than AI systems at predicting bare outcomes, so the word "expert" may carry little.
Without private, unpublished cases it becomes what a forecasting site already does.
One outcome is a weak score for a piece of reasoning. People are often right for the wrong reasons.
The legal class of a prediction contest varies by state.

blocks.text: **The drill-target challenge**

items: Far too few scored outcomes for the money: five holes from the one Australian precedent, none positive.

blocks.text: Two different records share this page, and they come out differently.
The record

**General average.** Under an old rule of the sea, if a ship and what it carries face a shared peril, and saving them costs money or means giving up some property, the cost is split among all those whose property came through, according to what each had at stake. A specialist called an average adjuster works out who pays what. The result, the adjustment, is a long document that sets out the facts, lists each expense, says which rule allows it, values the ship and each cargo, and divides the total.

A worked example from a real case. The container ship Yantian Express caught fire in January 2019. General average was declared [one-line-yantian]. Before any container was released, each cargo owner had to give a bond, and with it either a guarantee from an insurer or, for uninsured cargo, cash: 32.5% of the cargo's value towards salvage and a further 28% towards general average [yantian-notice]. That is 60.5% of the value [yantian-notice], held until the adjustment is finished. The final adjustment then says what each party owes and what is refunded.

**Demurrage.** When a ship is hired for a single cargo, the contract allows the charterer, the party hiring it, a fixed time to load and unload. Keep the ship beyond that and the charterer owes the owner a daily rate called demurrage. The file holds the contract, the ship's formal notice that it is ready, the port agent's timed log, each side's calculation, the letters between them and the figure finally settled.

An illustration, not a real file: the time allowed is 2 days and the rate is US$20,000 a day. The ship waits for a berth and it rains. The owner counts all the waiting and claims 3 days of demurrage, or US$60,000. The charterer says the notice was invalid and leaves out the rain, making it 2 days of demurrage, or US$40,000. They settle at US$50,000. The file holds both sums, the dispute between them and a single figure paid.
Why it might matter for training AI

Both records turn a contract and a messy timeline into a number that the other side accepted or disputed. That fits what vendors' pages show labs asking for: long office work with a check that is hard to game.
Neither kind of marine claim was found being bought by a lab or a vendor.
Who holds it and who may share it

**General average.** The adjusting firm keeps the file. The shipowner, the insurers and the salvors hold copies. The international maritime law body's guidelines say the surveyor acts for everyone with a stake, "any of whom are generally entitled to view all his exchanges of correspondence and reports" [cmi-guidelines]. So the adjustment circulates among the parties. No source showed that an adjuster may license it to outsiders, and no confidentiality rule was found in the text of the adjusters' association rules that was opened [aaa-rules].
No count of adjustments a year was found. As a sign of scale, a Lloyd's report counts 754 uses of its standard salvage contract in the ten years to 2013 [lloyds-lof].

**Demurrage.** Owner and charterer each keep a file of their own. In Australia the holders are the large shippers of iron ore, coal and grain. One Western Australian council puts demurrage at a single jetty at A$70 million a year [dcn-kwinana].
The contracts are private and commonly carry a confidentiality clause; the standard clause text was not read. One side could not share the whole file without the other.
Who is already there

**Demurrage is taken.** Marcura, a claims-processing company, says it handles "20,000+ claims a year" [marcura-service]. It says its system was "trained on more than 700,000 documents" and tracks "which charter party clauses generate the most write-downs" [marcura-blog]. A second firm, Burmester & Vogel, says its engine is "validated against 18k+ real laytime calculations" [bv-laytime]. Two voyage-software companies, Veson and Voyager Portal, manage claims inside their products, from tracking through calculation to invoicing [veson] [voyager].
So settled outcomes are already collected and used. What does not exist is a public test or a set offered to labs.
**General average is untouched.** No dataset, test, paper or company applying AI to adjustments was found.
What would have to be stripped
Little is personal: crew and surveyor names, signatures, agents' emails. The sensitive content is commercial: freight and demurrage rates, insurers' positions, the other party's documents.
Removing names is not enough. A fire on a known ship, or a queue at a known port on known dates, can be matched to shipping news and public ship-tracking data.
What stands in the way
**Demurrage**

items: The firms that process the claims already hold the outcomes. Whether their customer contracts would let them license the data was not established.
No buyer has been shown, and shipping is on no list of what labs want.
Each file has two sides, and disputes go to private arbitration.
The arithmetic is done by fixed-rule software. What is left for an AI system is reading the contract and the log, which may be too easy to be worth buying; this was not tested.

A qualified adjuster would have to check every case, so the cost to build is close to the likely price.
The adjuster's right to share a finished adjustment is untested.

blocks.text: Two small-business ledgers share this page and get different verdicts.
The record

**Vending.** The machines stand on premises that belong to others, and their owner, the operator, travels a round to restock them. A small modem in each machine reports every sale, stock level and fault. The ledger holds, for each machine, the layout of products and prices, every sale with its time, every restock visit, each price or product change, write-offs and the commission paid to the site.

An illustration, not a real file: a machine in a hospital corridor sells 60 colas a week at A$4. The operator raises the price to A$5. Sales fall to 50 a week, so weekly takings rise from A$240 to A$250. The operator then halves the restocking visits to one a week, the cola runs out on a Thursday, and about 10 sales are lost. Decision, response and cash result sit in one ledger within weeks.

**Bookmaking.** A bookmaker's trader sets the odds on each runner and moves them as money arrives. The ledger holds each price offered with the time of each change, each bet taken, the amount the book stands to lose on each outcome, the closing price just before the event starts, and the result. The trade treats the closing price as the best estimate of the true chance.

An illustration, not a real file: a trader opens a horse at $5.00. Two customers known to be well informed each bet $400. The trader cuts the price to $4.00. By the start the horse is $3.50 elsewhere. The cut was in the right direction and too small. The horse wins and the book loses $3,000 on the race.
Why it might matter for training AI

**Vending.** The best-known test of whether an AI system can run a business over a long stretch, Vending-Bench from Andon Labs, simulates exactly this trade. Andon says of it that "daily sales are simulated based on equations that can be gamed" [vending-bench-2]. The original paper says an AI system invents the three demand numbers behind each product [vending-bench-paper]. A real ledger could ground that simulation.
**Bookmaking.** The closing price is a fast, hard check on a forecast.
In neither case was a lab or vendor found buying such records.
Who holds it and who may share it
**Vending.** The operator owns the ledger. The telemetry company processes it.

One published term cuts against sharing. The terms that Nayax, one such company, sets for its developer interface list as prohibited "Selling, licensing, or purchasing DZ Data", defined to include "data anonymized, aggregated or derived from such data" [nayax-devzone]. On that wording, an operator that draws its own records out through the interface may not sell them. Nayax's main terms of service were not opened, and other telemetry companies' terms were not found.

**Bookmaking.** The bookmaker owns its ledger. Customer accounts are personal information. One racing-industry article counts 371 registered bookmakers in Australia in 2024 [the-straight]. The on-course trade has been shrinking: the bookmakers' association told Parliament around 2011 that it represented about 600 on-course bookmakers and that their share of turnover had fallen from 9.3% to 2.8% in a decade [aba-submission]. Licence conditions were not opened. Whether on-course ledger software keeps a timed history of every price change, or only the bets struck, was not established.
Who is already there

**Vending.** Andon Labs runs real AI-operated machines with Anthropic, so it has a small real ledger of its own [project-vend-2]. Real sales data has been used in research: one forecasting paper draws on a Chinese operator's 3,023 machines and more than 30 million transactions [usff-paper]. It holds sales only, without the operator's restock and price decisions. Nobody was found selling real decision ledgers.

**Bookmaking.** The checkable part is public and already packaged. PuntersEdge, an Australian service, offers "every price move for a race, per runner per book" across 15 racing bookmakers, with closing prices and results [puntersedge]. Public tests already score AI systems against betting markets. One, covering 104 football matches, reports that "none beats the market's Brier score", a standard measure of forecast accuracy [wc2026-agents].
A bookmaker's own ledger adds only what is private: the bets, the customers behind them and how the book was balanced.
What would have to be stripped
**Vending.** Very little. Card details sit with the payment processor. Site names and addresses would go, since a site's contract may make its sales confidential.

**Bookmaking.** A great deal. Customer names, account numbers, betting histories and credit balances are personal. Bookmakers also mark their winning customers, which is the most informative field and the most sensitive.
What stands in the way
**Vending**

items: The ledger records sales at whatever prices the operator set. It does not show what would have sold at other prices, so a demand formula is still needed.
The natural buyer already runs real machines.
At least one telemetry company's terms bar selling the data.

blocks.text: **Bookmaking**

items: Prices, closing prices and results are public, and an archive of them is already on sale.
The private part is customers' betting data.
Small on-course books may hold no timed record of price changes.
No buyer was found. Whether labs avoid gambling data was not established.

blocks.text: Two records share this page and get different verdicts.
The record

**Heir searches.** Sometimes a person dies leaving no will and no known close relatives. The lawful heirs then have to be proved. A probate genealogist reconstructs the family from certificates of birth, marriage and death and from other records, across countries, until every entitled person is identified and found. In the file are a log of the research, the certificates, the argument for every link, the dead ends and the finished tree. Then a court, an insurer or a public trustee accepts the tree or rejects it.

A worked example, from a case the New South Wales public trustee published with the name changed. "Max" died without a will in 2017 with four known siblings. Because his father had been born in England, certificates were ordered from there. They "revealed Max's father had a further five children with three different partners" [nswtg-genealogy]. Some certificates were missing, so the trustee applied to the Supreme Court, which "confirmed entitlement in accordance with the research done by the team" [nswtg-genealogy].

**Debit memos.** Travel agents book flights in a reservation system, often by typing terse commands. If an airline's auditors later find a ticket broke a fare rule, or used the wrong commission or tax, the airline bills the agency for the difference. The bill is called a debit memo. The agency pays or disputes it. The record is the commands typed, the booking, the fare rules that applied, the memo and the reason code on it, and the outcome.

An illustration, not a real file: an agent changes the date on a ticket and collects a A$150 change fee, misreading a rule that also required the fare to be re-priced. Months later the airline sends a memo for A$400. The agency disputes it, the airline rejects the dispute, and the agency pays.
Why it might matter for training AI

**Heir searches** are long investigations across many kinds of record, with dead ends, and a court's acceptance as the check. **Debit memos** are a record of software use marked by an outside auditor with money attached.
In neither case was a lab or vendor found buying the record.
Who holds it and who may share it

**Heir searches.** The trustee or the research firm owns its file. The New South Wales trustee said in 2022 that it was "administering over 2000 intestate estates, 745 of which involve overseas research" [nswtg-nowill]. Where a matter goes to court, the judgment is public and sets out the tree and the reasoning.

Much of the evidence comes from sources used under licence. The Australian terms of Ancestry, in the 2017 version that was opened, allow its content to be used "only for personal or professional family history research" and say "Resale of a work or database or portion thereof is prohibited" [ancestry-terms]. The conditions on registry certificates were not opened.
**Debit memos.** Every ticketing agency holds its own memos. The typed commands are held by the reservation system; whether agencies keep their own logs was not established.
The numbers are large but old. An airline industry working group reported about 2.35 to 2.4 million a year worldwide in 2015 and 2016 [iata-adm-2017]. Nothing newer was found.

The reservation systems' terms are the obstacle. Amadeus's standard terms say the subscriber "shall not compile, cache, sell, distribute or otherwise make available" Amadeus System Data except as expressly permitted [amadeus-terms]. They also bar using the system to train any "third party in the use of the Amadeus System" [amadeus-terms]. The screens an agent sees contain fares and rules, which are system data. The standard agency terms of the other two large systems were not found.
Who is already there

**Heir searches.** An open-source project, cowork-genealogy, gives an AI system research skills over a free genealogy service, and its repository includes an evaluation harness [cowork-genealogy]. It is free. No company or dataset using closed probate files was found.

**Debit memos.** Start-ups already sell tools to agencies. Aidah says its product, which sits inside Amadeus, brings a "90% reduction in ticket-related ADMs" [aidah]. No sale of command or memo data to labs was found.
What would have to be stripped

**Heir searches.** Living heirs appear by name in every file, along with their birth dates and addresses, who their parents were, and any adoptions or births outside marriage. Removing the living removes the last generation of the tree, which is what the search was for. How Australian privacy law treats the dead was not established.
**Debit memos.** Passenger names, passport and loyalty numbers, contact details and card fragments. Airlines' private fares and commission agreements are confidential.
What stands in the way
**Heir searches**

items: Take out the living and the answer goes with them; leave them in and privacy is breached.
A free tool of the same shape exists.
The evidence is licensed and cannot be passed on whole.
Published judgments may already have been read by AI systems.
No buyer was found.

blocks.text: **Debit memos**

items: The reservation systems' terms bar compiling or distributing what appears on screen.
Tools for writing commands and preventing memos are already on sale.
A usable practice version would need a working imitation of a reservation system with real fare rules. That is the real cost; the agency's files are a small input.

blocks.text: Three unrelated records, looked at more briefly than a full dossier. Each gets its own verdict.
The record

**Repair video.** Independent shops fix phones and laptop circuit boards by replacing parts a few millimetres across under a microscope, and a camera is often already fitted to it. What gets recorded is the footage, the technician's diagnosis, the parts used, and the outcome on the job ticket: the device starts or it does not.

An illustration, not a real file: a phone will not charge. The technician finds a short circuit, locates a faulty part by the heat it gives off, removes it and tests again. The phone starts. About 30 minutes of video and one yes-or-no result.

**Fire predictions.** During a bushfire, an analyst draws a map of where the fire front will be in the hours ahead, by hand or with a simulator. The truth arrives later as the mapped edge of the burnt ground. A real example: for New Year's Eve 2019 the New South Wales Rural Fire Service published a spread map for fires around Sydney showing "the communities that may come under threat from embers or fire fronts" [rfs-nye-2019]. Prediction and outcome are both shapes on a map, so the check is how far they overlap.

**Film cost reports.** Each shooting day a film production issues a plan and a progress report saying what was shot and what caused delays. Each week its accountant reports spending against budget. All of these go to the completion guarantor, an insurer whose promise to the financiers is that the film will be delivered.

An illustration, not a real file: a 30-day shoot is budgeted at A$6 million. By day 12 the unit is a day behind after bad weather and the forecast final cost is A$6.4 million. After a visit from the guarantor, a location is cut and two scenes become one. The film finishes at A$6.1 million. The record shows the plan, each day's slippage, each intervention and the final number.
Why it might matter for training AI
**Repair video.** Data vendors' pages show robot builders paying for recordings of skilled manual work. No lab was found buying microscope repair video, and no robot was found doing this work.
**Fire predictions.** An objective check, but the more likely customers are fire-technology companies and insurers.
**Film cost reports.** A long project with a forecast that can be marked against the final cost. No buyer was found.
Who holds it and who may share it
**Repair video.** The shop owns its footage. The device's owner owns any personal data that appears when the device starts.
**Fire predictions.** State fire agencies hold them. They are public bodies. Whether they keep the predictions they issue was not established.

**Film cost reports.** Film Finances, a guarantor, says its archive "contains production material relating to over 600 films that the company guaranteed before 1980" [film-finances-archive], and that it welcomes ideas for using it. A historian who worked in the archive describes "budgets, scripts, financing and distribution contracts, production schedules, progress and cost reports" [eup-blog]. Its Australasian arm says: "We are emailed each day's Call Sheet and Daily Progress Report. We are copied on weekly Cost Reports" [film-finances-au].
The production company owns the reports and the guarantor keeps copies. Whether the guarantor may license them for training AI was not established.
Who is already there
**Repair video.** Nobody was found pairing microscope video with the job outcome.

**Fire predictions.** No collected set of analysts' predictions against outcomes was found. A 2020 review says checking of both hand-drawn and simulated predictions "is not systematic" [fire-review-2020].
**Film cost reports.** Film historians have used the archive. Nobody else was found using guarantors' files: no dataset, no test, no AI company, no data broker.
What would have to be stripped
**Repair video.** Lock screens, notifications, photos and serial numbers that show when a device starts.
**Fire predictions.** Nothing personal. The difficulty is institutional: a scored archive would show where predictions fell short on days when people died.

**Film cost reports.** Cast and crew names, pay, injuries and notes on conduct. For the oldest files the sensitivity has faded; for current productions it is acute. Scripts in the files belong to others.
What stands in the way
**Repair video**

items: Similar video is already collected and sold at low cost overseas.
Robots do not do this work, and so no lab is known to want the footage.

blocks.text: **Fire predictions**

items: Timed maps of the true fire edge exist for few fires.
Agencies have reason to refuse.
No lab buyer was found.
Hand-drawn prediction is giving way to simulators.

blocks.text: **Film cost reports**

items: No buyer for estimate-against-actual project records was found.
The guarantor may refuse, or may lack the right to grant a licence.
The open archive is decades old and on paper.

blocks.text: This page is about a market more than a record. It describes the trade in introductions between companies willing to license their internal records and the firms that buy them.
The record

What is bought and sold is a working company's internal history: email, chat, shared drives, the customer database, the accounting ledger, support tickets, call recordings and code. The buyer takes a copy under licence, strips out names and personal details, and either passes the result to an AI lab or builds practice tasks from it.

Around that sale a second trade has formed. A referrer finds an owner who is prepared to license a copy, and introduces the owner to a buyer. The buyer pays the owner for the records and pays the referrer a fee. The referrer never holds any data.

A worked example, from terms the buyers publish. micro1's referral page offers "up to $50K" for each company referred, depending on its size [micro1-referral-page]. Its written terms say that where no amount is listed, the fee is 7.5% of what the buyer pays for the licence or purchase [micro1-terms]. Handshake's page says "Refer a company, get $10K", paid "when their deal closes" [handshake-referral]. In each case the referrer is paid only after the owner's deal has closed.
Why it might matter for training AI

Data vendors' pages show labs asking for the records of ordinary companies, and the buyers are advertising for them. micro1 announced in October 2026 that it would commit US$1 billion over twelve months to acquiring company data [micro1-commitment]. That is the company's own statement.

Confirmed prices are much smaller or not yet final. SimpleClosure, which sells the records of closing startups, says more than 350 companies have listed and forecasts returning more than US$10 million to them by the end of 2026 [simpleclosure-pr]. In the bankruptcy of Spirit Airlines, three firms have bid for the airline's records: Google US$10 million and Mercor US$7.5 million at auction [spirit-docket], and micro1 US$12.5 million in a later notice [micro1-bid]. The court has approved none of them.
Nobody was found who could be shown, publicly, to have been paid a referral fee. The promises are written down; proof of payment is not.
Who holds it and who may share it

The records belong to the company that operates. Hosts such as Microsoft, Google and Slack merely store them. Only the company can license them, through an officer with authority to sign. micro1's terms require the referrer to have the consent of "an authorized representative of the Company" before submitting it [micro1-terms].

Owning the records is not the same as being free to sell them. A law firm's note from October 2026 says: "A company that holds data does not necessarily have the right to sell it. Email and chat contain other companies' confidential information, often covered by NDAs" [fkks-note]. In the Spirit case a software supplier objected that, under its contract, data generated by its service belongs to the supplier and not the airline [spirit-docket].
Responsibility stays with the seller. Tonic.ai, which strips personal data for such sales, puts it this way: "The legal liability does not transfer with the dataset" [tonic-blog].
Who is already there
The market is crowded at every layer.

items: **Buyers with published referral terms:** micro1, Handshake. The General Data Company says only that "terms are agreed case by case" [general-data-licensing].
**Buyers with a referral button and no published amount:** a third-party survey found Mercor had "no published company-data referral terms as of 7 October 2026" [selldatatoai].

blocks.text: The terms settle how firmly the fee is owed. micro1's say it may "withhold, delay, reduce, condition, set off against, or refuse to make any Referral Payout... for any reason or for no reason", and may "require you to repay any Referral Payout already made" if a deal is unwound [micro1-terms].
What would have to be stripped

The law firm's note lists what an owner has to think about before selling: other companies' confidential material, legally privileged advice, and staff messages [fkks-note]. It says California's privacy law treats a paid transfer of workplace data as selling personal information, unless the data fits that law's definition of de-identified, and that staff messages about pay and conditions may be protected under American labour law whether or not the staff are unionised [fkks-note]. Those are the firm's readings; the statutes were not opened.
The Spirit case shows the argument in practice. The flight attendants' union objected that the sale would convey "substantially the entire employment and workplace record" [afa-objection].
What stands in the way

items: At the largest buyer the referral fee is payable at the buyer's discretion and can be taken back.
No paid referral has been publicly shown.
The only confirmed prices are small, or are bids a court has not approved.
Buyers advertise directly to the same owners. Credit depends on a tracked link.
An owner's lawyers may refuse, most of all where staff belong to a union or work in California.
The Spirit hearing was moved to 6 November 2026, according to one press report [travel-weekly]. No order has been made. The ruling, or action by a regulator, could change the market quickly.
If a sale goes badly for an owner, the blame falls on whoever made the introduction.

blocks.text: This page is about a market more than a record. It asks who already sells the records of failed companies for training AI, under whose authority, and at what prices.
The record

After a company fails, all that it wrote comes under the control of an officer supervised by a court: a trustee in the United States, an administrator or liquidator in Britain, Ireland, Germany and Australia. The officer's task is to raise money for creditors from whatever the company had. What is bought and sold here is the estate of documents: email going back years, contracts, invoices, ledgers, staff files and code, and, where the industry is regulated, what was filed with the regulator.
The trade has two shapes, so there are two worked examples, both real.

*Large and run through a court.* Spirit Airlines' estate auctioned its records, described as de-identified, on 14 August 2026 [spirit-docket]. Google bid US$10 million and Mercor was named as the alternate at US$7.5 million [spirit-docket]. micro1 later filed notice of a bid of US$12.5 million [micro1-bid]. Six objections and supporting filings followed [spirit-docket]. The hearing has been moved to 6 November 2026, according to one press report [travel-weekly]. No bid has been approved and no money has changed hands.

*Small and one bid at a time.* 1Day Sooner, an American non-profit, bids at the bankruptcies of biotechnology companies for the complete file that a drug company submits to regulators [1day-sooner]. By a press account it holds three such sets, two of them donated; two bids in 2026 were not accepted; and it estimates a non-exclusive copy at "a few tens of thousands of dollars" [mit-tr]. A foundation gave it US$500,000 in September 2026 to prove the approach [mit-tr].
Why it might matter for training AI

Data vendors' pages show labs asking for the records of ordinary companies and for tests an AI system cannot have seen. A failed company's records were never on the open web, and there is no live business to protect.

The General Data Company, an intermediary, lists the forms it sells: document archives, structured extracts, practice tasks, and held-out evaluation sets, and says estate data never appeared online [general-data]. Raw estate records have been sold, in small deals. For estate records sold as a private test, no sale was found anywhere.
Who holds it and who may share it
The estate owns the records. The intermediary acts as its agent. The firm that strips personal data works for one side or the other.

In the United States a sale of this kind goes before the bankruptcy court. The statute was not opened here. In the Spirit case the flight attendants' union argues that the privacy review was built for customers and that the sale would convey "substantially the entire employment and workplace record" of staff [afa-objection].

For Germany and the European Union, The General Data Company says: "The insolvency administrator controls the estate's assets, including its data. Licensing proceeds only under a written mandate from the administrator" [general-data]. Its pages cite no statute and name no administrator.
Suppliers may claim part of the estate. A software supplier objected in the Spirit case that records generated by its service were its own [spirit-docket].
The Australian position is on this site's page about closing companies in Australia.
Who is already there

items: **The General Data Company** offers the "document estates of wound-down European companies" [general-data]. It publishes no prices, buyers, estates or volumes. Its seller document puts first samples two to four weeks after an agreement [general-data-pack].

**SimpleClosure** closes down American startups and sells their code and workspace records. It says more than 350 companies have listed, and in September 2026 it opened to operating companies as well [simpleclosure-pr].

**Petrarch**, a young American company, says: "We source data including codebases, project files, and payments from bankruptcy courts, then de-identify and prepare the data for model training" [petrarch]. It names no case.
**Tonic.ai** strips personal data as a service, under the line "Turn a wind-down workspace into a licensable asset" [tonic-usecase].

blocks.text: Only the courts make an estate's price public. Each of the intermediaries has added a second source of supply, from live companies.
No Australian operator was found.
What would have to be stripped
Customers' details first. In the Spirit case, press reports say the passenger booking databases were removed and Tonic.ai was engaged to strip the email [piq-markets].

Staff records are the open question. micro1's bid offered to leave out the employee material the unions named, to keep the data in the United States, and never to transfer it to "any Chinese entity" [micro1-bid].

Stripping also collides with the sale contract. As filings describe it, the Spirit agreement promises that no part of the assets "has been deleted, modified, or removed" [micro1-bid]. An estate cannot easily promise completeness and remove what objectors want removed.
What stands in the way

items: The Spirit ruling. A refusal, or an approval loaded with conditions, becomes the template other estates' lawyers read.
The closest comparable names no buyer and no price.
The cost of checking rights and stripping personal data is large against the price of a small estate.
A non-profit that intends to publish what it buys removes exclusivity, which is much of the price.
