title: Failed companies' records sold as data

blocks.text: The record

This record has to be made. A person is given a task in real software: reconcile a bank feed, build a financial model, dimension a drawing. Their screen is filmed while a log captures every click and keystroke on the same clock. At the end something decides whether the work is right, either a marking scheme or an automatic check on the finished file. One attempt, with its video, log and score, is called a trajectory. What would be sold is a set of trajectories, ideally with many people attempting the same task, so a buyer can see how human results spread.

An illustration, not a real file: a monthly bookkeeping contest sets a task on a made-up company. Three transactions are coded wrongly and one is entered twice. A contestant works through 40 lines of the bank feed, posts a refund to the wrong account, sees the balance is out by $200, finds the slip, reverses it, and submits after 30 minutes. An automatic check compares the closing balances with the answer key: all four faults fixed, placed 20th of 100. The unit for sale is that half-hour recording with the wrong turn left in, the score, and the 99 other attempts.
Why it might matter for training AI

Some AI models now operate a computer the way a person does, by reading the screen, moving the mouse and typing. They are called computer-use agents, and they learn from demonstrations. Vendors' pages show labs asking for office-software work, for checks that are hard to game, and for records in which someone goes wrong and recovers. A scored contest attempt has all three.

Plain recorded hours have been shown to sell, on the sellers' own word. Markov says on its Y Combinator page that it has sold recordings of experts at work to frontier labs [yc-markov]. No seller publishes a price. No sale of scored recordings from a contest or an exam was found.
Supply is already running ahead of price. p(doom), a research lab, has released more than 600 hours of its own members' screen recordings free for any use [pdoom].
Who holds it and who may share it

Certification exams come closest to the record. Certiport, a Pearson VUE business, runs exams taken inside the live application for Microsoft Office, Adobe, Autodesk and Intuit software, and says it delivers over three million tests a year [certiport-facts]. Its customers are mostly schools, so many candidates are children. Exam owners guard their questions, and no recording product exists.

Proctoring firms, which watch candidates remotely, hold recordings but do not own them. ProctorU told the US Senate in 2021 that the test providers own the session recordings and that it does not use candidates' data to train its own algorithms [proctoru-senate].

Competitions are small and keep files, not recordings. The Financial Modeling World Cup, which also runs an Excel championship, had 363 participants in 2023 [wiki-fmwc]. Contestants upload a finished spreadsheet; its rules do not say that ordinary rounds are screen-recorded [fmwc-rules]. Its terms forbid reproducing any part of its website without written consent, and treat competition case files as confidential [fmwc-terms].

Paid recording programmes own whatever their contributors assign to them. A contributor can license a demonstration only if nothing on the screen belongs to an employer or a client. Ownership is clean only when the recording is made on practice data the organiser controls, by a person who has signed a licence.
No Australian holder was identified; local exams were not examined.
Who is already there

Sellers of human recordings are numerous. Datoric lists a set it describes as 250,000 traces with human-reviewed success and failure labels [datoric]. Chakra Labs pays people for recorded sessions in spreadsheet and design tools through a browser add-on called Pango [pango]. Paradigm Shift AI, Luel, fiund, Gerra and Realset list similar goods with prices on request [paradigm-shift] [luel] [fiund] [gerra] [realset].

Spreadsheet modelling, the obvious first subject, is already tested in public. One benchmark turned 113 of the World Cup's cases into questions and answers [alpha-excel]. BlueFin sets 131 finance spreadsheet tasks, and the best model scores under 50% [bluefin]. On FrontierFinance, human experts score 77.2% and the best model 70.9% [frontierfinance].
What was not found is anyone selling many people's attempts at the same task with an objective score attached.
What would have to be stripped
Names, and anything from a webcam or microphone: faces and voices raise biometric-privacy questions this dossier did not examine in law. Children's attempts are out altogether.

The larger risk is other people's property on the screen. WIRED reported in January 2026 that contractors for OpenAI were asked to upload real work from past jobs, and quoted an intellectual-property lawyer saying the lab was "putting itself at great risk" [wired-upload]. The Wall Street Journal reported that Mercor faces class actions after a breach exposed workers' facial data and screenshots of their computers [wsj-mercor].
What stands in the way

items: Plain recordings are being given away, and nobody has shown that a score earns a premium.
Spreadsheet modelling is already covered by several public tests, and models are close to expert scores on some.
Labs can generate traces from their own agents.
Contests draw hundreds of people, not thousands.
Exam bodies and proctoring firms are closed by ownership and by the secrecy of exam questions.
Software companies' terms on recording their screens are unread.

title: Scored recordings of people doing practical computer work

blocks.text: The record

Three related records sit under this heading. The first is a company's own staff using an AI assistant: what they asked, what the AI answered, and what they changed before using the answer. The second is the usage log of a company that sells a product built on someone else's model, such as a legal or coding assistant. The third is a programmer's session with a coding agent. The full log of one session, from instruction to outcome, is called a trace.

An illustration, not a real file: an accounts clerk at a distributor copies a supplier's statement into the firm's AI assistant and wants it reconciled to the ledger. Back comes a table: ten lines matched, three it cannot explain. The clerk sees that two of the three are one credit note entered twice, says so, gets a corrected table, changes one figure by hand and posts the entry. The record is the request, the first answer, the objection, the second answer, the hand edit and the posted entry. What matters most sits in the middle of that chain: the AI's error, and the fix a capable person applied.
Why it might matter for training AI

A lab cannot simply use its own business customers' logs, because its contracts forbid it. Anthropic's commercial terms bar it from training models on what customers put through its services [anthropic-terms]. Microsoft says prompts and responses in its Copilot product are not used to train foundation models [ms-copilot]. Business use is therefore traffic the labs carry but may not learn from. Only the customer can release it.
One buyer asks for it in terms. micro1, which buys company records, says it wants people's feedback on what AI produced in real workplaces [micro1-partners].
There is a counter-argument. Most logged use is the model getting something right, which teaches little. The useful slice is failures and corrections, and nobody has measured how large that slice is.
Coding-agent sessions are offered for sale. No priced sale of any company's AI conversation logs turned up.
Who holds it and who may share it

For business AI tools, the customer owns and the tool-maker processes. Anthropic's terms say the customer keeps all rights to what it puts in and owns what comes out [anthropic-terms]. Cursor, a coding tool, says that with its privacy mode on it will not train on customer data, and that with it off it may [cursor-privacy]. JetBrains collects detailed code data from companies only when they opt in, and says it will not sell or share it [jetbrains-faq]. OpenAI's wording was not read in full, so its position is not established here.

There is a catch. Anthropic's terms also say a customer may not use the service to build a competing product, including to train competing AI models [anthropic-terms]. That clause concerns what the service produced. The human side of a log, meaning the requests, objections and hand edits, is the customer's own work. Whether selling logs for testing rather than training falls outside the clause was not established.
Companies that sell AI products hold their users' sessions under their own customer contracts. Most that sell to businesses promise not to train on customer data, which also stops them selling it.

In Australia, the privacy regulator's guidance on commercial AI products says that where a new use of personal information is outside what people would reasonably expect, an organisation should seek consent or offer a real chance to opt out [oaic-ai]. How the Privacy Act's exemption for employee records applies was read only in commentary and is not established here. Nobody in Australia was found selling, brokering or buying such logs.
Who is already there

Magma, a Y Combinator company, connects to an AI product's database, packages its traces and corrections, and says it licenses them to labs for a share of the revenue [magma]. Cookiy Labs sells real coding-agent sessions, corrections included, with secrets removed on the developer's own machine [cookiy]. SourceX lists human feedback and scored work licensed for evaluation [sourcex].

JetBrains takes such data for its own models and pays in kind: free licences to selected companies willing to share edit history, prompts and AI responses [jetbrains-blog]. It is a buyer for itself, not a reseller.
What remains open is the everyday use of general-purpose assistants by staff at ordinary companies, corrections included. It is asked for but not yet shown sold.
What would have to be stripped

Prompts contain whatever staff pasted in: customer records, contracts, health details. The account holder cannot give consent on behalf of other people whose words appear in a log. A class action in California, *In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation*, is brought by meeting participants who say their conversations were recorded and used to train a transcription service without their agreement [otter-docket]. A separate complaint makes a similar claim against Granola [granola-complaint].
The AI's own output may also have to come out, if the buyer is a different lab from the one whose model wrote it.
What stands in the way

items: Labs and tool-makers already see the traffic.
Most logs record the model succeeding. The correction slice may be small.
The competing-model clause takes the AI's outputs out of any sale to a rival lab.
Personal and client information runs through the prompts, and lawsuits over meeting recordings are live.
Go-betweens are already in place.
No priced sale has been shown.

title: Records of people using AI at work, and correcting it

blocks.text: The record

This is a market, not a found record. A leading lab commissions practice tasks from a vendor, each with instructions, a working environment and a checker that marks the answer. The lab trains on the set until its model passes nearly all of it. The set is then called saturated, and the lab stops using it. The idea examined here is a second sale. A weaker model might still learn from a set the leaders have used up, so the buyer could be an American lab behind the leaders, a lab in China, or a business tuning a small open model. Goods sold this way, to many buyers from a catalogue, are called off-the-shelf.

An illustration, not a real contract: a vendor builds 500 spreadsheet-modelling tasks for a leading lab, using its own experts and marking schemes. A year later it repackages the same task designs as a catalogue item. A lab abroad sends vendors a list of subjects it wants covered, and the vendor licenses the catalogue item to that lab and to three others. The decision that matters is the repackaging, and the vendor makes it, because the vendor holds the rights.
Why it might matter for training AI
A model one step behind the leaders can still learn from tasks the leaders have outgrown. That is the whole case.

The trade has been reported at scale. Forbes reported in August 2026 that American data vendors, among them Surge, Mercor, AfterQuery and Turing, sell training data to Chinese labs, and that Chinese buyers ask for the datasets American labs have already bought [forbes-china] [lavx-summary]. The article was read here only in its opening and through other outlets' summaries, so its figures are left out.
Who holds it and who may share it

As a rule the dataset stays the vendor's and the lab is licensed to use it. Only one such contract is public, and it is clear on the point. Under Proximal's standard terms, what it delivers remains Proximal's own property, and the customer's licence is for internal use and cannot be transferred or sub-licensed [proximal-msa]. No other lab or vendor contract was read, so how typical this is has not been established.
On those terms:

items: A lab cannot resell a set once it is done with it.
A vendor can, unless it sold the lab exclusive use, and then only once the exclusive period ends.

For a company's raw internal records, the company keeps ownership and the buyer holds a licence. The General Data Company tells sellers that its holdings may be licensed again to later buyers as time goes on [tgdc-pack].
A reseller standing outside this chain owns none of it, and would need written permission from a vendor that already has its own sales staff.

blocks.text: On selling to China, the law is thin. Lawfare wrote in September 2026 that almost no law governs how data providers deal with Chinese AI companies [lawfare]. One rule reaches some data. The US Justice Department's Data Security Program, in force since April 2025, prohibits selling or licensing bulk sensitive personal data about Americans to persons linked to China, and its guidance says the data counts even when it has been anonymised [doj-guide] [ecfr-202]. Tasks written by experts that contain nothing about any individual appear to fall outside it, on Lawfare's reading [lawfare]. The volume thresholds in the rule were not read. No bill or new rule extending the programme to training data was found.
Contracts are moving ahead of the law. In its bid for the records of a bankrupt airline, micro1 promised that the assets would never be sold or passed to a Chinese entity [spirit-bid].
No Australian holder is relevant.
Who is already there

The vendors that built the data are the resellers: the companies Forbes named, and others. Scale AI is reported to have walked away from a Chinese contract over national-security concerns [fenado-summary].

Marketplaces fill the go-between role. DataVendor, provided by HUD, matches sellers' data, code and technical expertise with AI companies that need training and evaluation supply [datavendor]. Protege pools data from rights-holders and licenses each item to more than one buyer.
Chinese vendors are emerging to supply their home market [aiproem].
What would have to be stripped

Anything about real people, before a sale abroad: the Justice Department rule covers health, financial, biometric and location data and personal identifiers [ecfr-202]. A reseller also inherits every rights problem in the original set, including work files that contributors had no right to hand over.
What stands in the way

items: Vendors hold the rights and are already reselling. An outsider has nothing to hold.
A funded marketplace already takes the go-between's cut.
Sales to Chinese labs could be closed by a single extension of an existing rule, and the proposal has been written up in public.
Selling to Chinese labs is now covered in the press as a national-security problem.
Leading labs pay extra for exclusivity precisely to prevent resale.
Each resale needs fresh proof that the set still teaches the buyer's model.

title: Reselling datasets the leading labs have finished with

blocks.text: The record

Nothing here is found. It is built. What is sold is a body of tasks, a way to mark the answers, and a promise: the questions stay secret, so no model can have memorised them, and new ones are added on a schedule. A test of this kind is called an evaluation or a benchmark. It usually comes in three parts: a small public sample, a private part that can be licensed, and a private part only the owner ever runs.

A real example. Vals AI's Finance Agent test, in its second version, has 927 expert-reviewed questions about public company filings [vals-fabv2]. Of these, 27 are public, 450 form a private set offered for licence, and 450 are the test set, which Vals says will stay private [vals-fabv2]. When a lab hands over a new model, Vals puts the test set through a fixed procedure. Three AI judges mark every answer against a weighted list of checks, and the resulting score goes on a public table. The leading model scores 60.60% [vals-fabv2].
Why it might matter for training AI

This is less about training than about measuring. Labs want proof that a model has improved on work it has never seen. Companies want to know which model handles their own invoices, contracts or support tickets before they spend. Governments want measurement from someone independent.

Purchases have been shown here more clearly than for most records. Epoch AI says OpenAI commissioned 300 mathematics questions from it and owns them [epoch-frontiermath]. Vals, by its own account, is paid by labs to test their models, and raised US$40 million at a US$400 million valuation in August 2026 [vals-series-a]. LMArena, which ranks models by public vote and sells paid evaluations, raised US$150 million at a US$1.7 billion valuation in January 2026 [siliconangle-lmarena].

There is dissent. Tests published by data vendors are widely treated as marketing, and public tests that never change stop being useful once models have seen them. What is bought is trust and freshness, not the questions.
Who holds it and who may share it
Ownership follows the contract.

Commissioned work belongs to the lab that paid. Epoch says OpenAI keeps ownership of the questions it commissioned and that Epoch cannot share them with others without written permission; Epoch holds back 50 questions whose solutions OpenAI does not see [epoch-frontiermath].
An independent test belongs to its builder, who licenses parts of it or sells runs.
A test built for one company belongs to that company. PrivateEval sells on exactly that promise: the customer owns and runs the machinery, with criteria its AI suppliers never see [privateeval].

The raw material is the hard part. Refreshing a test takes a continuing flow of fresh real cases, which belong to whoever produced them. SourceX licenses business records for use in evaluation only [sourcex].

In Australia, the law firm Allens publishes a benchmark of AI models on Australian law [allens]. A one-person public project on Australian financial regulation has a five-item starter set [aus-reg-bench]. The Tax Practitioners Board has issued guidance on AI use but runs no test [tpb]. No Australian professional body was found running or selling one.
Who is already there

Vals says its tests appear in the model documents of the major labs, and it now offers a tool for building coding tests from a customer's own code [vals-series-a]. Epoch raised US$10.3 million in 2025 from donors and collaborators [epoch-report]. Andon Labs tests models by letting them run a real vending business [andon-vending]. Data vendors such as Mercor, Scale and Surge issue their own tests alongside their data sales.
Companies that build on the labs' models make tests too. Harvey's legal agent test has a public part and a held-back part, run by Vals, and the leading model scores 25.42% [vals-hlab].
For a company that wants to run its own tests, software is cheap. Braintrust lists a free plan, one at US$249 a month, and custom pricing [braintrust-pricing].
No price for a single benchmark, for a licence to a private part, or for a test built to order was found.
What would have to be stripped
Little, if tasks are written by experts or drawn from public material. If they are built from a company's real records, the same removal of names and client detail applies as for any business record.

Two risks are particular to tests. A leak destroys the product, so access has to be limited; Vals says it restricts the number of runs for that reason [vals-series-a]. And the tester is paid by the party it marks, a conflict of interest that an unknown tester cannot easily carry.
What stands in the way

items: Buyers pay for the name on the result. A newcomer has none.
Well-funded incumbents already cover law, finance, health and coding.
Australia-only content has few visible buyers; the one Australian legal benchmark is given away.
A fixed test goes stale within months, and refreshing it needs a secured supply of new cases.
Companies may not pay much when the software is cheap.

title: Private tests of AI, kept secret and regularly refreshed

blocks.text: The record

Bench science leaves a working record behind the published result. It has four layers. The first is the lab notebook, now usually electronic, in which a scientist writes what was planned, done and seen, together with the database that tracks samples and results. The second is the loop from a failed run to its fix: a robot script or a test goes wrong, the operator alters something, and the run is repeated. The third is the out-of-specification investigation: regulated manufacturers must formally investigate any result that falls outside the registered limit, recording the cause and retesting. The fourth is the dossier a drug company submits to a regulator, together with the study reports of companies that have stopped trading.

An illustration, not a real file: a contract manufacturer tests a batch of tablets. The strength test reads 94 against a permitted range of 95 to 105. The analyst and supervisor look for an obvious slip, such as a wrong dilution, and find none. Quality staff open a full investigation and suspect the reference sample the test is measured against has degraded. A second analyst retests with a fresh reference. Six retests all read about 100. The cause is recorded, the batch is released and a corrective step is logged. One case holds a stated problem, a chain of decisions and an outcome few would dispute.
Why it might matter for training AI

Biology is among the best-documented areas of lab demand, though much of the evidence is of talks and grants, not purchases. A brokerage news summary said in December 2025 that OpenAI had approached the lab-equipment company Revvity about licensing data and that other labs had opened talks with early-stage biotechnology companies [thefly]. The OpenAI Foundation gave US$500,000 to the non-profit 1Day Sooner to buy failed biotech companies' regulatory files in bankruptcy [pivotnews], and US$40 million to a university for cancer-vaccine data [mit-tr]. Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs jointly put US$300 million into a programme that generates data, and get a year's head start on what it produces [strategic-signal].

The answer on buying is split. Measurement data and regulatory files have named money behind them. The failed-run-and-fix loop and the investigation trail appear only in buyers' adverts. And the labs' own published work points the other way: OpenAI and Ginkgo Bioworks ran 36,000 reaction conditions over six cycles, with the model writing its own notebook entries [ginkgo-pr]. They made the loop themselves.
Who holds it and who may share it

Notebook software companies hold the data and their customers own it, but the companies have begun writing themselves rights. Benchling's enterprise agreement says the customer exclusively owns its data [benchling-msa], and its AI terms say it will not train models on that data without express permission [benchling-ai-service]. Its terms for free and academic users are different: a project switched to public view gives Benchling a permanent licence to distribute and sell that dataset, including for AI training [benchling-tos]. Dotmatics, which owns the notebook product LabArchives, says the customer keeps all rights in its data [dotmatics]. LabArchives keeps data readable for three years or more once a licence has ended [labarchives].

Contract labs and shared facilities hold other people's results. One Australian research institute's facility terms assign the intellectual property in the service to the customer on payment [cmri]. The national genomics facility throws samples away between one and three months after it delivers results, and keeps client records confidential [agrf]. What a facility can call its own is the log of quality checks and reruns, once clients' results are taken out.

When a biotech fails, the buyer of the drug usually takes the data with it. 1Day Sooner's fund therefore bids only for non-exclusive copies in American bankruptcies [ctd-commons]. In Australia, one listed biotech, Paradigm Biopharmaceuticals, entered voluntary administration in September 2026 [asx-paradigm]. How many Australian biotechs fail each year was not found, and the terms of Australian contract research firms and universities were not read.
Who is already there

Fallow Labs, which calls itself an AI lab, advertises for lab notebooks, test results, failed experiments and regulatory files, including from companies winding down; who stands behind it was not established [fallow]. DataNexx brokers lab-system and deviation records and pays the owner only if a licence closes [datanexx]. 1Day Sooner's fund says a non-exclusive copy of a regulatory file is worth tens of thousands of dollars, by its own estimate [ctd-commons]. Harell Data, which raised US$15 million in 2026, hosts biotechs' datasets so that model-builders train on them in place [geekwire]. Eli Lilly gives biotechs the use of its models in exchange for data contributions made through federated learning, which keeps their proprietary data private [revvity-lilly].
Well-funded science companies such as Periodic Labs and Lila run their own automated laboratories and do not buy.
No Australian seller or broker was found. Nor was anyone selling the troubleshooting loop as a scored product.
What would have to be stripped

Anything at the level of an individual patient; Fallow excludes such records from what it asks for [fallow]. Names of staff. Third parties' trade secrets, such as a customer's recipe inside a contract lab's files. DataNexx itself warns owners that research contracts, licences and grant terms can bar licensing even of data they hold [datanexx]. Work on dangerous pathogens or toxins may be unsellable.
What stands in the way

items: Labs and science start-ups generate the loop themselves, with clean rights.
The buyer of a failed company's drug, or its lender, usually takes the data exclusively.
Contract and licence terms block much of the rest.
The notebook software company may sell the pooled data itself.
One lab's troubleshooting may not transfer to another; nobody has shown that it improves a model.
Observed prices for a dead company's science are small.

title: The working records of biology laboratories

blocks.text: The record

Security service firms make four records. The first is alert triage. A security operations centre is the team that watches an organisation's alarms. When an alert arrives, an analyst runs a series of searches over the logs and then closes it as false, harmless or genuine. What is kept is the alert, the searches in order, the notes and the verdict. The second is the penetration-test report, from a paid and authorised attempt to break in: each weakness found, the proof, the client's fix and the result of the retest. The third is the incident timeline, an hour-by-hour account of what responders found and did during a breach. The fourth is a recording of a test call, in which a tester phones staff pretending to be the IT desk and tries to obtain a password.

An illustration, not a real file: in the small hours an alert fires because a finance employee appears to have signed in from two distant countries. The analyst first pulls that person's recent sign-ins and finds an unfamiliar device. A second search of the mailbox finds a new rule forwarding mail to an outside address. A third looks for the same source address across other users and finds two more. The analyst escalates. Next day the client's own team confirms a stolen password. The final label matters less than the three searches and the reason for each.
Why it might matter for training AI

Labs pay for tests of what their models can do in security. Forbes reported in September 2025 that Irregular, which tests models for OpenAI and others, had raised US$80 million at a US$450 million valuation [forbes-irregular].

The labs' own conduct in 2026 says more. Under Project Glasswing, Anthropic gave selected organisations its strongest model with up to US$100 million in usage credits [anthropic-glasswing]. Its Cyber Verification Program covers operations-centre and incident-response work and states that data retention is required for enrolled organisations, and gives the reason as monitoring for cyber misuse; it does not say the retained data is used for training [anthropic-cvp]. OpenAI runs a comparable access programme for banks and security companies [govinfosecurity]. The labs are getting live security work to pass through their own models by giving access away. They were not found buying archives of past work.

One finding runs in the record's favour. Alert-Bench, an academic test published in October 2026, replayed 1,247 alerts through a working log system and found that every AI approach it tried missed at least 40.4% of the alerts tied to an attack, mostly because it did not fetch the right evidence [alert-bench]. The analyst's sequence of searches is the missing skill.
No purchase by a lab or vendor of triage records, test reports, incident timelines or call recordings was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

The client owns its logs and the report it paid for. The service firm owns, at most, its analysts' methods and notes, subject to the client contract. No such contract was opened, so that split is not established in detail.

The profession has a rule. CREST accredits many testing firms, and its code of conduct covers penetration testing, incident response and operations centres. It requires members to keep confidential the data and research from earlier assignments and not to use them in other assignments, and not to disclose client information to any third party without the client's specific approval [crest-code]. Reuse without the client's consent is therefore barred outright.

In Australia the two largest providers now belong to overseas groups. CyberCX, with about 1,400 staff, announced in August 2025 that Accenture had agreed to buy it [cybercx]. Tesserent was bought by Thales in 2023 [thales-tesserent]. Sekuro, an independent, says it has more than 800 clients [sekuro]. No Australian provider was found selling its records or saying it trains on them.
Who is already there

The large security companies use their own data. CrowdStrike says its triage assistant was trained on millions of real decisions from its managed service [crowdstrike-pr]. Microsoft has given away a public dataset of 1.6 million alerts and 1 million incidents with customers' triage labels from 6.1k organisations [guide-paper]. It holds labels, not the searches behind them.

Specialists such as Irregular sell tests and practice environments to labs, not found records. Penetration-test reports that clients chose to publish are free to read, one project extracts their findings for model training [redblue], and made-up reports are published for the same purpose [synthetic-pentest]. One company sells a test run entirely by AI, so the report is becoming a machine's output [turbopentest].
Nobody was found selling real analysts' search sequences. Their holders are not free to sell, and those able to use them produce their own.
What would have to be stripped

Logs carry usernames, network addresses, email subjects and sometimes passwords and keys. A report on a weakness that has not been fixed is a weapon in the wrong hands. Breach reports are often commissioned through lawyers and may be legally protected; the Australian law on that point, and on recording phone calls, was not opened and is not established here. The person on a recorded test call did not agree to any resale.
What stands in the way

items: The client owns the record, and the profession's code forbids reuse without the client's approval.
Through their access programmes the labs already see live security work, and they retain it.
The large security companies sit on millions of labelled decisions, and one of them has released a large set free.
Funded specialists already hold the relationships with the labs.
Security data goes stale quickly.
The largest Australian holders are owned offshore.

title: The working records of cybersecurity firms

blocks.text: This page covers three unrelated records that share one feature: an outside party later says whether the work was right. They reach different verdicts, so each is marked throughout: **H** for home warranty, **L** for lawyers' negligence, **T** for test laboratories.
The record

**H.** Three Australian states, New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland, make builders take out state-run insurance for every home they build. Should the builder die, vanish or become insolvent, the scheme pays for the house to be finished or repaired. The claim file holds the owner's claim, an inspector's itemised list of work to be done (the scope), quotes from several builders against that list, the chosen quote and what was finally paid. A second file, on the builder, holds the accounts the insurer used to decide how much work that builder may take on. The verdict there is whether the builder later fails.

An illustration, not a real file: a builder is wound up when a house has only its frame standing. The scheme's inspector writes a scope. Five builders quote against it, from $180,000 to $240,000. The owner picks one at $200,000. Mid-job the new builder finds rotten framing that was not on the list, and the final cost is $220,000. So the file runs from scope to five prices, to the price chosen, to the sum paid.

**L.** Every solicitor must carry insurance against their own mistakes, in most states from a single mutual insurer tied to the law society. A solicitor who makes or fears a mistake notifies the insurer. The claim file holds that notice, the documents from the original matter, the insurer's estimate of cost, its defence lawyers' advice and the outcome. The Victorian insurer publishes anonymised cases of this kind for teaching.

**T.** A maker submits a product to an accredited laboratory to test whether it gives off, or suffers from, radio interference, or whether it is electrically safe. If it fails, an engineer changes the design and it is tested again. The record is the design, the measured failure, the fix and the passing retest. A physical instrument gives both verdicts.
Why it might matter for training AI

Each is professional work with a hard check attached: a price against what was paid, a lawyer's file against a finding of error, a design against a measuring instrument. Vendors' pages show labs asking for checks of that kind.
No purchase of any of the three by a lab or a vendor was found.
Who holds it and who may share it

**H.** The holders are the owners: three state bodies. In New South Wales the insurer icare received 749 new claims in a year and covered 23,943 builders [icare-ar]. It invites up to five builders to quote on each claim [icare-quoting], and pays Equifax to run its checks on builders [icare-ar]. In Victoria the insurance authority received 14,342 claims over five years [vago], and responsibility moved to the Building and Plumbing Commission in July 2025 [bpc]. In Queensland, claims for unfinished homes rose from 212 to 730 to 1,387 over three years [qbcc-ar]. The builder who finishes a job owns its own quote and invoices, and the homeowner receives the inspector's report. The state privacy and public-records laws were not opened, so whether any agency may license claim files is not established.

**L.** The insurer owns its claim file, but the documents inside it came from a client's matter. The Victorian insurer opened 514 matters in a year, of which 261 were claims [lplc-ar]. The New South Wales insurer received 714 notifications in a year, by the prior-year figure in the Law Society's 2024 annual report [lawsoc-nsw-ar]. The rules protecting a client's communications with a lawyer were not opened for this dossier. The working assumption is that the protection is the client's to give up, not the insurer's; that is not established here.

**T.** The manufacturer owns the report and the laboratory is bound to secrecy. The international standard that laboratories are accredited against treats information obtained during testing as confidential unless the customer has made it public [iso-17025]. One Australian laboratory's terms pass ownership of the report to the customer on payment and forbid the laboratory to disclose it without the customer's written consent [emctech-terms]. Only the manufacturer can license it.
Who is already there
**H.** The agencies run the quoting themselves, and Equifax runs the builder scoring. Neither has shown any wish to sell.

**L.** The holders already give the lessons away. The Victorian insurer publishes risk guides and case notes [lplc-ar]. Florida's insurance regulator publishes a database of closed claims against lawyers, with 8,175 entries [florida-study]. Harvey has released a legal test of more than a thousand tasks openly [harvey-lab].

**T.** Passing reports for certified radio devices are public in the United States. Failures and fixes are not, and nobody holds them pooled. Two young companies sell software that works from a customer's own reports: Crado ranks the likely causes of a failure [crado], and Fuchsia manages the compliance process [fuchsia]. Free tools predict interference from a circuit-board layout [kicad-emc].
What would have to be stripped

**H.** Homeowners' names, addresses and hardship notes, and builders' and their directors' finances. A builder's accounts are hard to disguise from anyone who knows the trade. In December 2025 the Victorian Ombudsman published a report on how that state's insurer handled claims after a large builder collapsed [vic-ombudsman].
**L.** Nearly everything: client confidences, settlement terms, and details of vulnerable clients.
**T.** No personal information. The sensitive content is the design itself, and a fix often reveals a weakness in it.
What stands in the way

items: **H:** the owner is a government agency under public criticism with no reason to license; no buyer has been shown; the work is already done in-house.
**L:** the client's confidence stands between the file and any sale; the lessons are free; open legal tests and a public claims database remove the scarcity.

**T:** manufacturers guard design files, so consent will be partial; no buyer has been shown; judging whether a different fix would also have worked needs scarce engineers; two start-ups are asking the same customers for the same files.

title: Three files with an outside verdict: home-warranty claims, lawyers' negligence claims, and failed product tests

blocks.text: The record
Two records were examined, along with a wider question.

The first is the working file of an Indian accountancy firm: the client's ledger balances, the items the auditors tested, the queries they put to the client, review notes by the partner, the audit opinion as signed, the tax return and any later ruling by the tax office.

The second is what an outsourcing firm in India or the Philippines holds for clients abroad: processed invoices, reconciliations, medical-billing claims and payroll runs, with the client's acceptance or rejection of each.

The wider question is whether labs that are not at the frontier, meaning American labs a step behind, Chinese labs, and model-builders backed by a region or a state, buy local professional work at all.

An illustration, not a real file: a firm in Bengaluru audits a small manufacturer. A junior notices that year-end stock is 20% higher than the year before. The manager asks for the count sheets. The partner requires slow-moving items to be written down. The client objects, and the opinion goes out with a paragraph drawing attention to the point. A year later the tax officer's ruling accepts the valuation. From first decision to outside result takes more than a year.
Why it might matter for training AI

Accounting work with a later outside result is the kind of record labs are said to want. The hope was that labs behind the frontier would buy it more cheaply from countries where a great deal of such work is done.
Nothing found supports that. What the evidence shows instead:

items: Chinese labs are reported to buy tasks written by experts, and packaged datasets already sold to American labs, from the very American vendors that supply the frontier labs [lavx-summary]. The reporting describes tasks and packaged sets, not company archives.

India's model-builders work from customers' own data and state programmes. Sarvam sells tuning on a customer's own data and says that data is not pooled or used to train Sarvam's models [sarvam]. BharatGen, which is state-funded, is building a store of Indian-language data and cites more than 15,000 hours of annotated speech across 22 languages [bharatgen].

In the Gulf, Mistral and Humain announced a collaboration which they put at several hundred million euros and which covers Arabic models among other things [mistral-humain]. No data purchase was disclosed.
For Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia and Europe, one search found nothing on professional-work data. That is weak evidence of absence.

blocks.text: Who holds it and who may share it

**Indian accountancy firms.** The firm keeps its audit file. An earlier screen for this project recorded that the Indian accountants' institute bars members from disclosing client information without specific authority. The institute's code was not re-opened for this dossier, so its exact wording is not established here.
**Outsourcing firms.** The client abroad owns the records. The outsourcer is a processor, meaning it handles them only on the client's instructions.

**India's data-protection law.** The rules under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act were notified in November 2025, and its central duties, covering consent, notice and purpose, begin in May 2027 [dpdp-rules] [induslaw]. A law firm's summary says that an Indian firm processing foreigners' personal data under a contract with a party outside India is exempt from most of those duties [induslaw]. The Act itself was not read. If that summary is right, an outsourcer need not meet Indian requirements for its foreign clients' data. The exemption does not hand it any right to that data.
**The Philippines.** Its privacy law was not opened.

**Australia.** For Australian content, a single buyer has named a budget. Sovereign Australia AI says it has earmarked $10 million to acquire data, paying news services and buying books and music [sovereign-au]. The Copyright Agency reported in October 2025 that Australian AI start-ups, Maincode among them, had pledged to pay for the Australian content they use [copyright-agency]. For neither company was a signed deal or a sum actually paid found. No buyer of Australian professional-work data was found.
Who is already there

American task vendors sell into China [lavx-summary]. Vendors with staff in India sell expert labour and tasks to American labs; LH2 AI Labs, for one, says it supplies frontier labs and enterprises with rights-cleared datasets drawn from under-represented populations [lh2]. It publishes no prices, customers or list of datasets. It sells to frontier labs from India, and that tells us nothing about follower labs buying Indian files.
Chinese domestic suppliers are emerging. One of them, Benyuan Zhishu, organises professionals in mathematics, coding, law and medicine [benyuan].
Nobody was found selling professional files from India or the Philippines. The simple reason is that the holders are not free to sell them.
What would have to be stripped

Indian tax and audit files carry national identity and tax numbers, bank details and salaries. Once those go, little is left. Outsourcers' archives carry other countries' personal data, including American patients' records, under contracts whose breach would end the outsourcer's business.
What stands in the way

items: The holder has no right to sell: the profession's code and client contracts stand in the way.
No buyer has been shown for foreign professional files. Follower labs want what frontier labs have already tested.
Brokers of company records that state a preference ask for English-language, American companies first.
Take the identifiers out of an Indian tax file and little of substance remains.
Selling toward China carries a cost in standing with American buyers.

blocks.text: This page covers five ways of making a record that would not otherwise exist, or could not otherwise be licensed. They reach different verdicts, so each carries a letter throughout.
The record
A created record exists only because somebody arranged three things beforehand: permission, a way to capture the work, and a later check on the result.

items: **A. Own a business.** The operator of a small real business owns everything it produces: quotes, jobs, ledgers, staff messages, results.
**B. Give away software.** A tool a business uses every day, for meeting notes or bookkeeping, whose terms give its maker a licence to what passes through.
**C. Trade a discount for rights.** A firm that installs AI for a client charges less and keeps a copy, with identities removed, of the inputs, steps and results.
**D. Pay professionals.** A person supplies a finished piece of real work, with the request that prompted it, under a licence.
**E. Run a panel.** A business owner records a real decision while its result is still unknown, then reports months later how it turned out.

blocks.text: A real example of D. OpenAI's GDPval test is made up of 1,320 tasks drawn from 44 occupations, every one built on real work that someone produced [gdpval]. The professionals who wrote them averaged 14 years' experience, were paid at least US$40 an hour, and each task went through five rounds of expert review [gdpval-paper]. The average task in the core set takes a professional 404 minutes, worth US$361 at median wages [gdpval-paper].

For E, an illustration, not a real file: the owner of a 40-person freight firm records that she will raise prices by 10% on a large but barely profitable customer, and puts the chance of acceptance at 60%. Six months later she reports that the customer accepted 8%. Because the entry was closed before anyone knew the answer, no model can have come across it.
Why it might matter for training AI

Vendors' pages show labs asking for real work with the process visible, for expert judgement with reasons, and for tests no model has seen. They also show buyers checking where a record came from. With created data, every item can come with its own proof of consent. Most found data cannot offer that.

D has been bought, by action: OpenAI built GDPval this way [gdpval], and WIRED reported in January 2026 that its contractors were being asked to upload real work from past jobs [wired-upload]. For A, labs have reached such data by taking ownership stakes or lending staff; nothing was found showing cash paid for the data itself. For E, no buyer was found.
Who holds it and who may share it
Ownership is fixed by contract at the moment of creation, which is the point of the category.

items: **A.** The business owns its records, subject to its contracts with customers and its privacy promises to them.

**B.** The user owns its data; the software maker has only the licence its terms grant. JetBrains, the nearest precedent, collects detailed data from companies only when an administrator switches sharing on, and says it will not pass the data to third parties [jetbrains-faq].
**C.** The data stays the client's, and a copy is licensed.

**D.** The catch is the employment contract. Handshake asks contributors for documents they own or are authorised to share, and Inc. noted that most employees do not own the documents they create at work [inc-handshake]. Someone who owns the business, practises alone, or freelances with rights retained is placed differently.
**E.** The owner owns what they write and the documents of their own business.

blocks.text: The Australian privacy and workplace-surveillance rules that would bear on A and B were not opened.
Who is already there

**A** is occupied by capital. OpenAI took an ownership stake in Thrive Holdings, which buys accounting and IT-services firms, and placed its own research and engineering teams inside the group's companies [reuters-thrive]. General Catalyst says it generally invests upwards of US$100 million in each such business [gc-services], and that one of them, Long Lake, has made 40 acquisitions [gc-longlake]. Andon Labs runs a real shop in San Francisco with an AI manager; the shop had lost US$40,000 by August 2026 [sfstandard].

**B** has a single precedent, and the data there stays with the software maker. JetBrains gives free one-year subscriptions to selected companies willing to share data for its own models [jetbrains-blog]. No free software funded by reselling users' data was found.
**C** is described by one insider as a growing line for the largest vendors. No second source was found.
**D** has posted prices. Handshake offered US$6 a page for up to 50 documents of up to 100 pages each, capped at US$30,000 a person [bi-handshake].

**E** is nearly empty. Metaculus runs forecasting contests for AI systems [metaculus-bots], and sells paid forecasters' reasoning with prices on request [metaculus-pro]. No one was found selling logged decisions with their outcomes.
What would have to be stripped

Customers' and clients' names from any work document. Staff, pay and health details. In D, anything that belongs to an employer: WIRED reported that OpenAI leaves it to contractors to remove confidential and personal details themselves [wired-upload]. In E, named staff and counterparties. Outcomes that people report about themselves can be wrong or flattering, so a document showing the result is needed.
What stands in the way

items: **A:** the capital needed is very large, and a lab's way in is an ownership stake, not a purchase of data.
**B:** a long build before any data arrives.
**C:** rests on one account; not a business alone.
**D:** contributors submitting work that is not theirs; and it is unproven that a finished task sells for more than it costs to make.
**E:** no buyer; one outcome is a noisy mark for one decision; people stop answering follow-ups.
**All:** sales of created data depend on trust and a strong sample, and a newcomer has no one inside a lab to vouch for it.

title: Records that must be made, not found

blocks.text: This page covers two unrelated records with different verdicts. Each is marked throughout: **A** for aircraft, **F** for forecasts.
The record

**A.** Two linked records exist for a small aircraft. The defect log records every fault that a pilot or an engineer reports, the action taken, and whether the repair was lawfully put off for a period. A repeat defect is the same fault coming back soon after it was signed off, which shows the first diagnosis was wrong. The second record pairs the reason a part was removed with what the workshop found when it stripped the part down. A finding of "no fault found" tells us the part was sound and the diagnosis was wrong.

An illustration, not a real file: a flying school's training aircraft is written up for a flickering charging light. The engineer tightens a loose connector and signs it off. Ten flying hours later the same fault is written up. The engineer removes the alternator and sends it away; the workshop tests it and finds nothing wrong. The fault is reported a third time, and this time the voltage regulator is changed, and the fault does not return in the next 200 hours. Three diagnoses: two shown wrong by later facts, one shown right.
**F.** A company forecasts its own cash or budget, saves the forecast at successive dates, and later learns the real figure.

An illustration, not a real file: in November a distributor budgets revenue of $4.0 million for the March quarter. In January it revises this to $3.8 million because a customer's order is late. In February it revises again to $3.6 million. The ledger later shows $3.5 million. Every version notes which assumptions moved and the reason. The check is the bank statement, and every version was fixed in place before the answer was known.
Why it might matter for training AI
**A.** Fault-finding with a physical check fits what vendors' pages show labs asking for: tasks whose marking is hard to game. No purchase of this kind of record was found.

**F.** Finance is among the most repeated requests. A forecast with a sealed date can be turned into a test: hand a model the company's books as they stood on the forecast date, have it predict the figure, mark that against the outcome, and set it beside the finance team's own forecast. No purchase of this was found either. But finance tests are being built quickly and the best AI systems fall well short on several. MBABench has 101 whole-workbook tasks [mbabench].
Who holds it and who may share it

**A.** In Australia the log belongs to the aircraft's registered holder. The Civil Aviation Regulations require the holder of the certificate of registration to maintain a log book for the aircraft and to make it available to the regulator and to people maintaining the aircraft [car-50a]. A schedule to the same regulations lets some sign-offs sit in either the log book or the maintenance organisation's own work records [casa-sched6]. The log therefore belongs to the owner or flying school, the job records to the maintenance shop, and the strip-down report to the overhaul workshop. Linking a removal to a finding needs two or three consents. Rules on how long records must be kept were not read.

For airliners the same information already flows to the manufacturer. Airbus's reporting guide asks operators for removal records and suppliers for workshop findings in a standard format [airbus-guide].

**F.** The company owns its forecasts outright. An accountant or software company only holds them. The weak point is the versions: many firms overwrite the file. Where versions survive is in dated documents such as monthly board papers, reports to lenders, and the document sets shown to investors. Two published checklists for such document sets list budget-against-actual comparisons as standard items [telegent] [aistartupcfo]. No law or software term was found that stops an owner licensing its own forecasts, though lender and investor confidentiality clauses were not checked.
Who is already there

**A.** A free public body of text exists. The US aviation regulator publishes each year's reports of malfunctions and defects as a downloadable file [faa-sdr], and the Australian regulator has a searchable service for major defects [casa-drs]. An open test for airliner maintenance, CAMB, has 7,969 multiple-choice items and 50 fault trees built from real troubleshooting cases [camb]. Several young companies review aircraft records with AI, but for the sale and lease of airliners and engines; one, TRecs, took an investment from an engine maker's leasing arm in May 2026 [businesswire-trecs]. None was found handling the defect logs of small aircraft, and none claims to sell data.

**F.** The tests that exist ask a model to build a spreadsheet model or explain a gap from numbers it is given. BlueFin has 131 finance spreadsheet tasks, and the best model scores under 50% [bluefin]. On FrontierFinance, experts score 77.2% and the best model 70.9% [frontierfinance]. FINCH built 172 workflows partly from the files of Enron, a company that failed in 2001, and the best model passes 38.4% [finch]. None scores a forecast against the eventual outcome at a real, privately owned company. That one of them reached back to Enron for real version histories suggests how scarce the material is.
What would have to be stripped
**A.** Pilots' and engineers' names and licence numbers, and the registration mark, which identifies the owner. Passages quoted from maintenance manuals are the manufacturer's copyright.
**F.** The numbers usually contain nothing personal. The commentary may name customers, staff and salaries.
What stands in the way

items: **A:** no buyer; a free public body of defect reports and an open test already exist; the records are handwritten and scattered; linking them needs several consents; each holder has little.

**F:** the versions may simply not exist, because files are overwritten; a single outcome is a noisy mark for one forecast, so many are needed; it appears on no buyer's list of wants; on short-range cash, models may already do as well as finance teams, in which case nobody needs the test.
